vice in competition with the Canadian Pacific Railway. Were it not that these other things were included in the charter I would not have voted for this clause.
There is no reason why they should not be covered by the General Railway Act.

This clause does not allow remuneration for services except to engineers or contractors, and I would regret if the clause were interfered with because in my experience of building railroads I have found it most valuable where your stocks or securities are not very good, and I regret to say that many of them are not good. In the case of the Georgian Bay branch of the Grand Trunk Railway, a lot of local enthusiasts, of whom I was one, built 200 miles, and we were only too happy to get the Grand Trunk Railway to take it over subsequently and operate it. We had no money in our early days and we issued stock and bonds for this purpose and we found it a very useful clause. In the days of the railway boom in Ontario we invested our money in building railway lines and we were glad to unload them afterwards on the Canadian Pacific and the Grand Trunk Railway. I got cured of it, but I learned a little about railways and the value of stock and bonds. Our great trouble always was to get in the unsuspecting capitalists whom we are now so much afraid we will impose upon. I believe that if the railway commission is worth a cent it will protect us, and that we, therefore, need not destroy one of the resources that is indispensable to build a railway line. I myself helped to pass this sort of a clause in 1888, and the Conservative government adopted it, and since that time, notwithstanding the thousands of miles of railway that have been built, we have not found any abuse coming from it. In the new clause which the Minister of Railways and Canals proposes in the Railway Act he still further restricts these powers. Is not this clause the same as the Minister of Railways and Canals will have in the new Railway Act.
It is founded on it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Does not the clause as it stands at present render it perfectly possible to give any proportion whatever of the capital stock of the railway company, as a bonus for placing the bonds. Would not that be feasible if you leave in the words ' or services rendered.'
Yes, it is covered by services rendered, except promotion services.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Has that been struck out ?
No. I said if the committee thought proper. I am not wedded to it at all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Why not strike it out ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: According to the rules of the House, an amendment cannot be made to a private Bill without one day's notice being given.
I think in any case this should be non-preference stock.
The answer applies which I gave to the hon. gentleman before. Section 39 of the Railway Act Is exactly the same as this, and has been in force since 1888.

The observation of my hon. friend from North Simcoe would be perfectly pertinent if the general Railway Act made provision for the issue of preference stock; but as it does not do that, his remarks have not very much importance.
I do not think it makes provision for the issue of any kind of- stock.

Then, this clause has an entirely different application from that in the Railway Act; because this Bill gives power to issue preference stock, and clause 11 is sufficiently comprehensive in its terms to include preference stock. I think the clause should certainly be amended in the way suggested by my hon. friend from Hamilton. I do not see what reasonable objection there can be on the part of promoters, because every object intended to be served by section 11 could be satisfied by limiting it to common stock.
I quite agree with the hon. leader of the opposition that if there is-any doubt, it should be made clear that common stock is meant, and I think the promoters would consent to that.
Would you not allow a contractor to be paid with preference stock ?

The object of issuing preference stock is to give a security, which is better than common stock. I imagine it could not have been contemplated by the promoters to ask for this, because it is a departure. I have not known that power to be given before. I certainly would vote against preference stock being allowed to be given; but if the committee thought differently, I would want to have it made plain that it could be either preference stock or common stock. There are serious reasons, I think, why a preferred security should not be applied in that way. The directors could apply bonds on their own responsibility without legislative authority. When the Bill went through the Railway Committee, no question of this sort was raised. If it had been, I certainly would have opposed the inclusion of preference stock.
Is there a clause in the general Railway Act allowing the issue of preference shares ?
No, nor common shares either.
Then, this must be limited to common stock.

With all due deference to the hon. leader of the opposition, I do not think his argument is good or valid. The interpretation clause does not contain the word ' stock,' and does not define or confine it. Whether it would be common stock or preference stock may be a debatable question; tout there is no limitation in the Railway Act, which has been in force since 1S88, so that I think the arguments which I advanced in answer to the hon. member for Hamilton are substantial. Of course, what the hon. member for South Norfolk says as to preferred stock not being used in this way in his experience is very strong. If it has not been so used, I do not suppose it will be used in this case. But I do not know what the intention of the promoters may be.

I cannot say that I look with favour on this method of using the stock; but I must confess that it would be particularly objectionable to my mind to use preference stock in this way. I think my hon. friend would do well to consent to the inclusion of the words, ' shares in the common stock of the company,' in the second line of the clause, so that it will be applicable to the ordinary or common shares.
Mr. McCarthy. Let that clause stand.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The amendment could be made by unanimous consent.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think not.
I think anything can be done by unanimous consent.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The reason for a day's notice being required is this. This is a private Bill, and there might be outside parties who, knowing that the Bill was to come before the committee to-day, and knowing this rule, would be absent, and hence could not be heard.
Outside parties could not be heard, anyway.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: They could through their representatives.

The Deputy Speaker is quite right in saying that we ought not to do anything in the way of amending a clause without notice, though I am quite sure we could do anything in Committee of the Whole by common consent. I remember the same question arising in connection with Hon. Mr. TISDALE.
the London and Port Stanley Railway Bill, in which amendments were made by the
member in charge of the Bill, with the common consent of the committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I will just read the rule.	'

Before you read the rule, might I be permitted to suggest that these rules for the business of the House are made for the governance and convenience of the members of the House, and not for the governance or convenience of any persons outside of the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Knowing that there is a rule which prevents important amendments being made in the Committee of the Whole, some members might not make it a point to be present as they otherwise would if they thought that any important amendment could be made. The rule is as follows :
No important amendment may be pressed to any private Bill in the Committee of the Whole House or at the third reading of the Bill unless one day's notice of the same shall have been given.
Bourinot says that the correct course is to refer the Bill back to the Select Committee to which it had been previously sent.
What is the object of our going into committee at all if we cannot change the Bill ?
Let me also say that the logical result of your ruling, Mr. Chairman, is that we never could suspend the rules of the House unless we had every member present in his seat.

I would ask to let the matter stand until I can find out whether the amendment is of importance or not. I do not know whether the promoters will consider it important or not.
Section allowed to stand.
On section 12, describing line of railway.

In the notice of application for charter, the eastern terminus was fixed at Gravenhurst. What has caused the company to change it to Moncton ? Also I find that this section, No. 12, contains these words :
Thence in a north-westerly and westerly direction passing to the north of Lake Nipigon, in the province of Ontario, to a point at or near the city of Winnipeg ; thence westerly and north-westerly, passing through or near Battle-ford. Edmonton and Dunvegan, or by such other more feasible route as is hereafter located, but following in a general direction that herein indicated, and by way of either the Peace River pass, or the Pine River pass, or such other pass in the Rocky Mountains as is found most convenient and practicable, to Port Simpson or Bute Inlet, or such other port on the Pacific coast between the said points as is considered more accessible and better adapted for the purposes of the company.

Wlmt does that mean ? Does it mean that they can go practically where they please so long as they get to the Pacific coast ? Is that the idea ? Will the hon. gentleman please answer these two questions-why was the eastern terminus removed from Gravenhurst to Moncton, and what is the meaning of these words I have just read ?
1 may inform the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) that I am not in the confidence of the managers of the Grand Trunk.
Do you know anybody who is ?

I am not able to tell why the terminus was removed. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) is a member of the Railway Committee and he remembers the discussion which took place at the time the eastern terminus was fixed at Moncton. So far as the other question was concerned, this is the usual clause inserted in a railway Bill. It permits construction from ' at or near' a certain point to ' at or near* another point. The reasons for this are obvious. A railway company when applying for a charter, cannot lay down their routes specifically. The protection of the public lies in the power of the Governor in Council or Minister of Railways and Canals, for every railway must locate its line, and that location must be approved.

I would like to ask the hon. promoter of this Bill whether it is the intention that this line shall be carried through the state oif Maine in going from the province of New Brunswick to the province of Quebec ?

As I understand the Bill, the only power given is to construct the line in Canada, I know of no other intentions on the part of the company. If such an intention exists, it has never been communicated to me. So far as I know, the intention is to build the line in Canada.

I do not think the hon. gentleman (Mr. McCarthy) has given a fair answer to my civil question, in giving the information he has given just now. I am quite aware, though the hon. gentleman may not be, that this parliament would have no authority to give the Grand Trunk people power to build through the state of Maine, and that is the only thing the promoter has given in answer to my question. And the point covered by my question was ' a point of some importance.
I do not think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) could have heard the last two sentences of what I said.

I say it is a matter of some importance to the people of New Brunswick, and to the people of the province of Quebec as well, to know if it is the intention of the Grand Trunk Company,
in carrying their line from Moncton up through the province of New Brunswick and Quebec to the city of Quebec, to build through the state of Maine or not. It would make a difference in the length of the route and also in the direction, and I think it is only right that the intention of the company should be stated to the House and to the country. And, if the hon. promoter of the Bill has not that information at hand he will have the opportunity to procure it from the persons who are behind this Bill before eight o'clock.
As I said, I am not going to build this road. So far as the intention has been communicated to me, the intention is to buiid the road through Canada-it is to be an all-Canadian road.

I do not observe anywhere in the Bill any obligation on the company to build any one of these sections. I think the Bill leaves it entirely open to build any of the sections the company sees fit to build. Is that the understanding of the Railway Committee when they reported the Bill ?
Mr. McCarthy. Several motions were .moved in the committee as to the constructions of these sections-first that they should be constructed simultaneously, then, one two, or three sections simultaneously. The committee had several votes on the subject, but the clause was left as the hon. gentlemen now find it. Of course, it was considerably different from what it was as introduced. But it was affirmed in this point by the committee after discussion, and, I think, four or five votes.

I may say that I myself moved an amendment to this clause providing for the simultaneous construction of all the sections, meeting the very objection taken by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax). It was urged in the committee at the time that if there was no aid given to the company it would not be fair to dictate to them what sections of the road it should build, and it was thought better to leave that until the Bill was introduced giving aid to the company, if such a Bill were introduced. We were told that if such a Bill were presented, we should have a full opportunity of discussing the matter and urging that the road should be constructed simultaneously from end to end. With that understanding, I asked to be allowed to withdraw the amendment I proposed. But, the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Cas-grain) objected to that, and there was a vote taken op my amendment much against my will, with the result that it was defeated. But I do not say that the vote upon that amendment represented the views of the committee at the time, because a great many of the members voted against the amendment I proposed simply because they desired to have the matter brought up when the

subsidy is discussed, if a subsidy Bill is brought before parliament. I think that some undue and improper comments have been made, and the country is not fully aware of what has taken place in the committee. We have uot receded from our position in the slightest degree that there should be some guarantee that the whole line should be built; at the same time it aids the construction, and it seems to me that if this were done, it would meet many of the objections brought forward this afternoon.

No doubt a great deal of the embarrassment felt by many of the members in dealing with the Bill had its source in the impression which had become general that this company would have aid in some form or other from the government. It was my endeavour, as it was the endeavour of other members of the committee to dissociate that question from the question before the committee. It might be ultimately that aid would be given, and it might be that it would not; and it was only lair to deal with this Bill upon the basis that no aid would be given, inasmuch as it might uot be given. It would not be fair to hamper the Bill with conditions which we would not impose upon another company.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Were not the company obliged to shift the terminus a thousand miles east of where they originally intended to have it.
That was the action of the committee. I was not in favour of it; but the committee felt disposed to do it and did it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Were not the members of this House justified in the belief they formed with regard to the prospect of government assistance to the road by the eloquent speech delivered by Sir Charles Rivers Wilson before the committee, wherein he distinctly said that he expected that the government were going to build the road ?

I do not know whether my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes. Victoria) expects an answer to that question or not. It did not alter my mind upon the question of what would be a proper action on the part of the committee. It was for the reason that the committee did not think that it ought to impose cdnditions, there not being any assurance that government assistance would be given, that the motion moved by my hon. friend from Annapolis (Mr. Wade) was voted down as also were other motions of the same character. I treated it simply as any other company asking for a charter would be treated, and I think that that is tlie principle upon which we ought to deal witli this Bill to-day.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do not entirely agree with what the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) has said that, as this is only a Bill providing for a charter, we have no right to impose conditions. When this company come here and ask for a charter they are asking for certain privileges which it is in the power of this House to grant them, and if we have a right to grant them, we certainly have a right to impose upon the company the conditions which we believe to be in the best interest of the country. We have a' right to impose any conditions we see fit ; and it seems to me this is a very reasonable condition, and the only test of its reasonableness is whether it is in the best interest of the country.

Would the hon. gentleman treat a Bill of this kind precisely on the same basis, whether the company was to get any assistance or not ? Would he annex conditions in the same way and oblige the company to go on and construct the work without any public aid whatever, just as he would if we were giving it aid ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I may say this, that in the case of the company receiving pecuniary assistance such as the minister speaks of, the conditions you would impose might be more onerous than the conditions you would impose when they were only asking for a charter. It depends entirely on what you are giving them as to what conditions you would have a right to impose. It is all a question of reasonableness after all. That is the standpoint from which I look at this question, when we are asked to say whether this company shall begin simultaneously at these different points, because they have divided this railway into different sections. Now they must have had some object in view when they made that division. Why not consider the railway as a whole ? Why not come here and ask for a charter over this line as a whole, to run from Port Simpson to Moncton ? Then the matter might be in a different position. But here they have divided their line into sections, and therefore they would have a perfect right, according to their charter, to ask for aid to build the prairie section, the section that would pay for itself, and leave the other sections unbuilt. Therefore we see this extension that was given as a sop to the maritime provinces, this extension from Que? bee
We should not complain if it has been given.

But if it is no good then we have a right to complain; if it does not fill the bill we have a right to complain. If it does not remedy the grievance which we are complaining of, then we have a right to complain, and that is the point I wish this committee to consider. Because there is no assurance, there is nothing in

tlie charter which compels these people to build from Quebec down to Moncton, and therefore if they are honest about this
Would the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him a question ? Does he complain because the Bill has been changed, and the eastern terminus has been made at Moncton instead of Quebec ?

I have no objection whatever to the extension down to Moncton, I am in perfect accord with that; but I want something more than a mere provision in the charter to assure me that it is going to be built. That may suit the hon. gentleman for Annapolis (Mr. Wade), but it does not suit me. I want to say here and now that the conduct of the gentlemen who were promoting this Bill before the Railway Committee was not such as to impress me with much confidence in their bona tides. I want to say that the lack of frankness with which these gentlemen replied to the reasonable questions that were asked them by men who were there representing their constituents, impressed me that they were not bona fide in their intention to build from Quebec down to Moncton.
^t six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
On section 12,

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Casgraiu) asked me to move the amendment of which he gave notice as follows :
That the said Bill be referred back to the Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines, with instructions to add to the said Bill, after section 13 of said Bill, the following :-*
Provided that in the event of the company receiving from the government of Canada any assistance, either by way of subsidies, moneys, land grants, guarantees, loans, or in any other manner whatever, the work of construction on the Quebec section be commenced simultaneously with the work on the woodland and prairie sections and be completed and put in operation simultaneously therewith and before the company exercise any of the powers conferred upon it by section 33 of the present Act in respect to ' lease and running powers over other railways.'
That motion might very well be moved when we are going into committee, but not while we are in committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: An hon. member may move that the committee refer back at any stage.

Ml'. Chairman, let me call your attention to the fact that the hon. gentleman's motion is to refer back to the Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines not to the House. Your jurisdiction only is to receive a motion that this
committee rise and report progress. This motion should have been moved in amendment to motion that the Speaker leave the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The rule is that the hon. gentleman cannot move now. The amendment is out of order.
May I ask the ground for your ruling, Mr. Chairman ?
As I understand the point takeii it is that this motion must be moved when the Speaker is in the Chair, and not when the House is in Committee of the Whole.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We have not the power to move in this committee that a certain Bill shall be referred to a committee of the House, but while the Speaker is in the Chair, this motion should have' been made that the Bill be referred back.

Before this section passes,
I wish to offer some remarks to the committee. I do not think, as a member representing a constituency deeply interested in this Grand Trunk Pacific scheme, in the project as a whole, and in its success, that I can support the passage of this clause through the House, as it stands, f objected to a certain provision in it in the Railway Committee, and I feel so strongly on the subject that I feel compelled to register my objection against it in the Committee of the Whole. I have more faith in the commercial success of this proposed Grand Trunk Pacific scheme than many of these who have already spoken on it seem to have. While they supported it in a measure, they declared themselves as of the opinion that it was not within the bounds of possibility that it should be a commercial success. For my part, if I did not think the scheme was a good one in the interest of the people of Canada and that it contains the elements of financial success,
I would not have abused the position which I hold in parliament of voting for it or supporting it. Believing that this is a good proposition for the country at large, and that it is a practicable business proposition, I feel bound to do my part at any rate to leave the proposition in a position whereby it shall have a reasonable chance, both of benefiting the country and turning out to the financial benefit of those interested in it. As I understood the policy of the government in regard to this scheme, as stared by the right hon. Prime Minister before the Bill was introduced, it was that there should be a transcontinental railway extending from tide water to tide water. To secure this transcontinental railway extending from tide water to tide water entirely on Canadian territory, it was expected that this country, according to the sanction of parliament, would be prepared to make very considerable financial sac-

rifiees. I am sure that parliament agreed as to the desirability of having a transcontinental railway entirely on Canadian territory extending from tide water to tide water, and not only from tide water to tide water, but from tide water on one shore to tide water and open navigation all the year around on the other shore. If this is desirable, and every body will agree that it is desirable, then it is most desirable that the shortest possible line between an all the year around ocean port on the Atlantic and an all year round ocean port on the Pacific should be chosen. It is necessary that this should be in the interests of the people who require to use the road, and it is just as necessary on the part of the people who are to own and operate the road. Every mile of length more than is absolutely necessary means increased cost in the building and increased cost in the operation. Somebody has to pay for that. It may be that the company is willing to agree to an unnecessary lengthening of the line, believing that the country will pay for the extra cost of building and operating that unnecessary length. And the company are perfectly right in believing that it is the country, either the national treasury or the ^producer who is to use the road in order to get his products to market, who actually has to pay this extra cost. If that should be the case, then when parliament is defining the route and the terminal points of this road, it is the duty of parliament to define the shortest route and the most available and suitable terminal points. I cannot support the section as it stands, which provides that the eastern terminus of this great transcontinental road shall be at a point where there is no ocean port; where there is no possibility of making an ocean port, and which will entail an unnecessary construction of 100 miles to reach a Canadian winter port, and a consequent increased cost of hauling. Owing to the number of rulings which have been made here to-day, I cannot tell whether I would be in order in moving a motion or not, but I propose to lay before the committee the suggestion that the word 'Moncton ' be changed to ' St. John,' so that parliament shall become responsible for indicating the eastern ocean port of this transcontinental road at the nearest and best port that Canada has in consideration of distance and other matters. I do not see how parliament can justify itself if it gives assistance towards the construction of a railway, the whole purpose of whose existence shall be to give Canadian ocean port facilities the year round, and then allow that road to be constructed to a point where there is no ocean port, and which is 100 miles from the nearest available ocean port, the construction of which to that point would increase the haul by about 200 miles.
Mr. GOURLEY, I want to move an amendment to that clause 12.

I object.
Mr. OLIVER,

Then I beg to give notice that on the third reading of the Bill I shall move that the Bill be recommitted for the purpose of inserting the following amendment :
Provided that in the event of the company receiving from the government of Canada any assistance, either by way of subsidies, moneys, land grants, guarantees, loans or in any other manner whatever, the work of construction on the eastern section be commenced simultaneously with the work on the Quebec, woodland and prairie sections and be completed and put in operation simultaneously therewith and before the company exercise any of the powers conferred upon it by section 33 of the present Act in respect to lease and running power over other railways.
1 can assure the promoter of this Bill that all we in the maritime provinces are desirous for is that we shall be assured that this Grand Trunk Railway, which has received from Canada enormous grants of money, shall have a Canadian eastern terminal, and so far as I am concerned I am willing that it shall receive more aid, provided it shall become a national highway in the true sense of the word. I would suggest to the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) that he should leave to the maritime members to determine upon the question of the eastern terminus. I would be perfectly willing to take his judgment with reference to the terminus in Alberta, but he ought to reciprocate, and take our judgment as to the eastern terminus. We do not propose that the road should stop at Moncton, because there is no very great sea-port there, but what we do wish is that there may be some common point in the maritime provinces upon which we can agree, and if the Grand Trunk Railway comes to Moncton we shall take chances afterwards as to which is the best port, whether it shall be Country Harbour, St. John or Halifax. I am not sectional enough to be wedded to any of these ports. All I want is that the products of this great country shall be sent to the markets of the world through a Canadian port, no matter which it be. I want the gentlemen from the west to be Canadians first. At this time in the history of Canada we should not know that there is a west or an east. For my part, I do not know that there is any boundary between Nova Scotia, New Brunswick or Ontario ; I know nothing about provincial boundaries, excepting as regards little provincial affairs with regard to the administration of mere local funds.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

There are no boundaries in this country for me except the Canadian boundary from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and from the 49th parallel to the Arctic ocean. This is all the country a Canadian should know, and every Canadian must reach that standard and be prepared to do everything that will develop Canada as a whole. We must understand that this railway company has already a large system of

railways operated in Canada. If this company had no port at Portland, I would be in a different position ; but it has enormous terminals there, and so far as I am concerned, I believe that by proposing to come to Moncton the Grand Trunk Railway are simply dragging a red herring in front of our noses so that when they get their charter and have their line built to Montreal they will give the go-by to the maritime provinces and say : Gentlemen, we have terminals at Portland, and we will use them. I can understand the promoters of this Bili being blinded by their surroundings ; I can understand one or two gentlemen in this House being blinded by their associations with the Grand Trunk Railway, but I cannot believe that the ordinary member from Ontario or from the west can be blinded by such considerations. I quite understand that any Canadian in this parliament should think and think only of making the Grand Trunk use a Canadian port. The time has come, and parliament might as well know it first as last, when the people of Canada will not put up any longer with a foreign port being used to export the great products of Canada. I am willing to vote any amount of money to develop the west; but I want the western members to see that it is a disgrace to Canada to have the great products of the west shipped at Portland. What will the world think of Canada if we use a foreign port ? It will say that Canada is crippled in its geographical area. It is a scandal to Canada, and will give a bad impression of the country abroad. Notwithstanding the fact that we have the best ocean ports if only they are exploited and used. The other day it was alleged in the Railway Committee that because Halifax or St. John was over 150 or 200 miles apart, farther from the west than Portland, that was an answer to the proposition to use a maritime province port. But I am prepared to show that two or three hundred miles at the end of a long haul is not the slightest obiectioii. There are railroads in the United' States which will carry the products of the country 3,000 miles as cheaply as other railroads will carry them 2,500 miles. Therefore, the gentleman who said that 200 miles of haul was going to destroy the value of a maritime province port as a great entrepot of this country, was not right in his statistics nor right in his heart-he was wrong at both ends. Now, Sir, I undertake to say that the time has come when this House should give the Grand Trunk formal notice, giving them one, two, or three years to make preparation to leave Portland. Is not this time for doing that, when they are coming to parliament asking us to make this system, which has hitherto been a purely Ontario system, a great north-western system ? They are asking us to extend their system into the great territories of the west, to enable them to bring grain
and dump it at Portland. In the early days when the Grand Trunk Company got its charter, there was not in Canada the national feeling that exists today ; the provinces were not confederated, there was very little hope that we would arrive at our present stage of development, and the Grand Trunk was allowed to make its entrepot at Portland. But now that is all changed. Canada has become a great country stretching from one ocean to the other, and there is no reason why the Grand Trunk should not be told, if you want this charter, you will have to take it on the express and clear condition that you shall use a Canadian port. I am in favour of the motion of the hon. member for King's, N.B. (Mr. Fowler), but it is inadequate. I do not care how many clauses you put into the charter, requiring the Grand Trunk to take their freight to a maritime province port. Unless the shipper routes them that way it is no protection, because the Grand Trunk can give the shipper a wink, and say, route all your stuff to Portland. We must meet this question like lawyers and men, in a way that will make it impossible for the Grand Trunk to budge from a Canadian port. Turn this question around. Suppose the Grand Trunk came here asking us to make Seattle, in Washington, their dumping port on the Pacific coast. I would fight as strongly for you in the west as vou should be fighting for us. You expect us-to stand up as one man and say that our Pacific slope shall not be abandoned, and the United States coast used and exploited by a great Canadian concern against the Intel ests of Canada. In the same wav I want all the members of this House to stand up and say that the maritime province ports of this country must be exploited and developed for the purpose of rounding out this confederation. I am bound to tell you that the whole maritime provinces are aroused over this question. I was home two or three weeks ago, and I never heard a question so thoroughly discussed up and down the streets, in Halifax, in Amherst, in Truro, as this question ; and every merchant, every workingman, every man in the streets, was of the opinion that the time bad come when the maritime provinces should stand up for their rights. I remember when the Canadian Pacific Railway was built, the Conservative party with which I was identified, had to meet the charge of all that money being expended in the western country.
How about the Intercolonial ?
Of course, that was our answer. I do not care where the money is spent if it is necessary that we should have a national highway over Canada, and we voted in support of the Canadian Pacific Railway.

Why not extend the Intercolonial westward ?
down

every province has its rights and privileges respected. I hope that the province or Quebec, the great province of Ontario, and the whole of the west will stand by the maritime provinces in the appeal we are now making.

My hon. friend from Colchester (Mr. Gourley) has spoken quite eloquently on the desirability of our having a Canadian national winter port instead of Portland. That is my idea as much as his, and it is because I desire to see such a result that I refuse to endorse a proposition which would unquestionably prevent its being achieved. This road must be given the shortest line to a Canadian port or commercial reasons will prevent it from using that port. Either St. John is that port or we have none. It is therefore our duty, if we have any such ambition, to provide that this road shall run to St. John and not run around 200 miles. But if the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway is built from Quebec to Moncton and if traffic is ever carried to a Canadian winter port, that carriage will be 200 miles longer than it need be. That certainly means that the freight will not be carried over that road. We may use means which will compel to a certain extent the use of our own roads to our own ports, but there is a limit beyond which we cannot compel trade to follow our channels, and that limit is passed if we compel freight to be carried 200 miles out of its way in a total distance of about 400 miles. The Intercolonial Railway is acknowledged to be working at the greatest possible commercial disadvantage because it does not run to St. John by the nearest possible route. Are we to repeat to-day the error made twenty years ago by allowing that port of St. John, which is Canada's nearest all the year around ocean port, to be hampered by chartering a railway to run around it a distance of about 200 miles ? Those who uphold such a proposition can only do it on the supposition that the Grand Trunk Railway will never be built between Quebec and Moncton. I would be very sorry to support such a proposition ; and it is because I cannot support it that I take the liberty of forcing my opinion on the House at this stage. I look upon this as a great national question. Although I am not from the maritime provinces, it is just as dear to my heart to see a Canadian port handle Canadian trade as it can be to the heart of any one down by the sea. But if that be our ambition, we must take the proper means to achieve it, and when we are giving a charter to and aiding a railway, let us do so in such a way that it will have a reasonable chance to accomplish the object we all desire to see achieved.
My hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Oliver) is not very conversant with the geography of the maritime provinces. I agree with the hon. member for Colchester that we would not presume in

the maritime provinces to dictate the course of any railway through the district of Alberta and set our views in that connection against those of my hon. friend. The first proposition of the Grand Trunk Railway was to build a road from Quebec and then use the Intercolonial Railway to Halifax. Having taken some little trouble to ascertain the distances between certain points,
I find that the difference in distances between C'haudiere Junction and Moncton by the Intercolonial Railway and by the proposed route from Chaudi&re Junction to Moncton, in as direct a line as possible, is 129 miles. We save 129 miles by building the road from Chaudi6re to Moncton in as straight line as possible.
How far is the whole distance from Quebec to Moncton ?

Three hundred and sixty-eight miles by the proposed route from C'haudiere to Moncton, and it is 497 miles by the Intercolonial Railway. This shows a saving of 129 miles on the proposed route to Moncton from C'haudiere as compared with the Intercolonial Railway. What I want to point out to my hon. friend from Alberta is this, that coming from Chau-difire to Moncton this road will pass through or near Chipman, N.B., and from Chipman there is a road already constructed to a point on the Intercolonial Railway near the city of St. John, so that when you are building this direct line from Chaudiere to Moncton, you come within fifty miles of St. John. Therefore my hon. friend's contention that we should use the port of St. John is met by the fact that the road will be completed to St. John when the proposed line is built to the town of Chipman.
I find by the Intercolonial time table that the distance from Quebec to Moncton to which he refers is 488 miles.

Then the leader of the opposition corroborates my original statement. Now, I say if you build the road from Chaudiere to Chipman you are then within about fifty miles of the city of St. John. If you contend that the port of St. John must be used for heavy freght, then you have your line to that port. But everybody admits that passenger traffic will actually come from the port of Halifax. Do you imagine, Mr. Chairman, that passengers coming from Liverpool to this country would desire to pass the port of Halifax and go on 300 miles through the tides of the Bay of Fundy to the city of St. John, when they could get off at Halifax and proceed west by rail ? Everybody admits that Halifax is the proper port for passenger traffic. Now, by building a road from Chipman to Moncton, a distance of less than fifty miles, you have got a railway from Chipman to Halifax. So when you build to this given point 163
of Chipman, you swerve to the right fifty miles to St. John, and to the left fifty miles to Moncton, where you join the Intercolonial and proceed to Halifax. We do not claim that Moncton is a port, of course, it is nothing of the kind; but it is a given point from which the traffic will travel to Halifax, and if you swerve off from Chipman, freight traffic will be taken down to St. John. Let me repeat this once more. You leave Chaudiere and go dowrn to the point called Chip-man. When you reach Chipman you are within fifty miles of St. John on the right and fifty miles from Moncton on the left. Now, Mr. Hays, the distinguished manager of the Grand Trunk, in his statement before the Railway Committee, said that* he could fill half a dozen ports with the traffic from the west. Then why do you want to confine it to the one port of St. John ? I am not here to make any criticism about the capabilties of the port of St. John, it has got the Canadian Pacific Railway terminus there at the present time, but I am here to state that there is no better port in the world than the port of Halifax. It has no high tides, it has no currents, it has no ice, it is a magnificent port, one of the most magnificent ports in the world. Now, by going to Chipman you can utilize the two ports, and if Mr. Hays' statement is correct that he can fill six ports, then you have more than one port, because you can go to Halifax as well as St. John, and my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Fraser) reminds me that there is also the magnificent harbour known as Country Harbour. I want to point out another thing, that when you come from the west to the east, you are 300 miles nearer to Liverpool when you get to Halifax than you are at St. John. When you get to Halifax you are on the ocean, you are out at sea, but when you get to St. John you are in the Bay of Fundy, which has sometimes tricky tides. Therefore it seems to me that in insisting that this terminus be made at the city of Moncton, you provide for utilizing the two great ports of Halifax and St. John-also Country Harbour.
What is the distance from C'haudiere to Moncton by the short line ?
It is 129 miles shorter.

I would like to say a few words also on this question. It always appeared to me that we were doing the proper thing in assisting the farmers in the west to relieve themselves of their surplus grain. To do that it is necessary, if we are to compete with the American lines, to afford as cheap a rate as the United States can give. Now, I believe in running a straight line from a point a hundred miles east of Lake Nipissing straight to Quebec. Certainly it will run through a good country,



a country that will be settled in the future, and a country from which I believe the railway will derive a good profit before long. Now, the great point for the maritime province people to consider is the route to be followed between Quebec and a maritime port. For myself I am in favour of the port of St. John. X am in favour of it because X am well acquainted with the advantages that that port possesses over any other. I do not say that our port is more handsome than any other, but I think that it affords shipping facilities of the very best order. Its excellence has been approved by disinterested men who reported in its favour for cattle shipment. The officers that were sent out by the British government admitted that there was no port on the Atlantic coast, which included every port in the United States, that possesses advantages for the shipment of cattle equal to those afforded by the port of St. John. I think the opinion of these disinterested men may be taken to be as near the truth as possible. I believe that if the line ran to St. John it would be better for the merchants of Canada. I do not say anything against the idea of turning'off and running to Moncton; but no man in this House can persuade me that It is advantageous, after reaching Moncton, to go 189 miles farther, a distance which is practically unnecessary. From Chipman to St. John the distance, we are told, is fifty miles; we are also told that it is fifty miles from Chipman to Moncton. I think the distance will be found shorter to St. John than to Moncton. However, when they arrive at St. John, goods can go on board ship, but when they arrive at Moncton, they have 189 miles further to go. Then we must consider that the cheapness of the transportation of these goods to Great Britain is the principal feature when we are endeavouring to compete with American lines. The freight can be carried from St. John to Liverpool as cheaply as it can be carried from Halifax to Liverpool. If there is any advantage, it is in favour of St. John. People who send steamers to St. John on speculation, irrespective of grain or other goods, are always sure of getting a cargo of deals, it matters not in what season of the year. For this reason, I oppose building a line that is adapted to business for only six months in the year while the other six months it will benefit the United States. Let us benefit ourselves all we can, consistently with the interest of business.

My geography, perhaps, is not as accurate as that of some of my critics, yet I do not think they came out very well in the display. I would like to say that in the figures I have taken down there is this difference ; the present route by the Intercolonial Railway between Quebec and Halifax is 129 miles longer than the proposed route across the province of Mr. TUCKER.
New Brunswick. Passengers, then, using the present Intercolonial Railway to Halifax have to travel 129 miles further than they would have to travel if this Moncton proposition is carried out. But, if I do not mistake the facts, even adopting the suggestion made by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan), freight will have to be carried about 100 miles further than it otherwise would be required to be carried in order to reach St. John. That is to say, taking a direct line, or as direct as possible, down the St. John valley to St. John, approximately, 100 miles shorter than going around even by Chipman, as he says. Now, I submit, that, as between 100 miles longer for freight and 129 miles longer for passengers, the interests of this country would be in favour of the shorter freight route instead of the shorter passenger route.

May I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) a question ? How does he make out that the freight route to St. John is 100 miles more ? Where does he get his figures ? I contend that his figures are not correct.

It is 89 miles from St. John to Moncton. This proposed point to Chipman is 50 miles from Moncton and 50 miles from St. John. Now, it must, therefore, be in the neighbourhood of 50 miles on the way from Moncton towards St. John. But it is 89 miles by a direct line from St. John to Moncton by rail. Then any point 50 miles from St. John and 50 miles from Moncton must be about half of 89 miles from St. John.
Oh, oh,
I am stating my position in answer to the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade), who asked me to give the basis of my calculation. According to my calculation, the position is as I state.
Have you seen the map V

Yes, I think I know as much about the map as the hon. member (Mr. Talbot). If Chipman is approximately about half as far east of St. John as Moncton is, it takes that much difference to get to Chipman, and that much back, and take the two together it makes approximately 100 miles. That can be noticed on the map as easily as it can be figured out, and there is no question about it. Let me further point out that the suggestion of running the road direct to Moncton involves the crossing of certain divides and lengthening of the road beyond an actual air line; whereas the proposition to follow the St. John river as much as possible gives not only a shorter line, but, probably a better grade. * Now, if it is a matter of so little account that the road shall reach the ocean port, that it shall go to a certain point and be spider-legged from there, why not just as well go to St. John and then take a short run around to Moncton and to Halifax. It is no further to

St. John from Moncton than it is from Moncton to St. John-I think lion, members will admit that at least. Then it is a reasonable proposition that the freight shall be carried to Moncton and then carried to St. John.
No, rro.
That was the argument before the Railway Committee. It is not Chipman which is desired to be the terminus.
They hare to go to Chip-man to get to Moncton.

That is no argument. There is a road down the St. John valley, so that it is just as far from Chipman to St. John. If it is so easy to run back from Moncton to St. John, it is as easy to run forward from St. John to Moncton. And what we who are interested in this railway from the point of view of those who furnish the traffic of the road and so are interested in the cost of service over the road, would ask is, wherever you run your road, run it by the nearest ail Canadian air line to a Canadian port-and that is St. John. It is not something that is to be decided in the future. Those cities have been there for a hundred years. The port of St. John is the best available port on the Bay of Pundy according to the facts before us. Why should we wait to find out something more ? Why spend years in waiting to find out, why spend millions of money to find out something which is known and known beyond peradventure for many years ?
Now, I would like to speak on the subject of sectionalism. It has been hinted that those who ask that the shortest route should be adopted are sectionalists, and the interest of the west and that of the east are said to be in conflict. In this case, the interest of the west and the interest of the east are one. I claim that the interest of both parties is to get the shortest line from the source of travel to the ocean port, from the ocean port to the field of supply. I did not raise this question of sectionalism. I stand here accused of sectionalism. Will the House believe me when I say that the members who set out to advocate this most remarkable proposition to go to Moncton, do not represent any part of the province in which it is proposed to run this road. If that is not sectionalism, I would like to be told what it is. We do not stand to be accused of sectionalism, by these hon. members at any rate, who, not being in a position to have the road built into their province, attempt to dictate to this great country where that road shall have its terminus. There is sectionalism for you. And not the provinces which must furnish the traffic for the railway, but the province which hopes to benefit from the traffic over the railway which nature has decided shall not be built 163*
within its limits. These gentlemen have appealed to the House on grounds of patriotism and nationalism. I hope they will take these appeals to themselves, because they are more fitting subjects for appeals of this kind than those of us who ask that this greatest of national questions that have come before parliament in recent years be decided on the broadest and most unquestionably national ground.

I am sure if I were to attempt to discuss the geography of Alberta I would make as many mistakes as has my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver), who has just taken his seat, in his reference to New Brunswick. At considerable pains I have worked out the distances by the several proposed routes. I find that from Chaudiere by way of Connor's Station, Ed-mundston, Boiestown and Moncton, the distance is 340 miles. A portion of this mileage is fixed by actual railways now constructed. There would be 276 miles of railway to be surveyed. Adding the usual percentage for curves, it would make the distance 368 miles. This information is obtained from what would be considered the most reliable sources in this Dominion. If you go by way of Connor's Station, Ed-mundston and Nashwaak bridge route, you have precisely the same result, 368 miles.	The St. John river route will
commence at Edmundston and run down the valley of St. John and reach Woodstock. It would then strike back through the country. It would go down the valley of the St. John to Fredericton, which is some 60 odd miles, and if it did not it would have to go to Fredericton junction and follow down, paralleling the present Canadian Pacific Railway.
Not at all.

My hon. friend from Sunbury (Mr. Wilmot) says not at all. I am sure it would not go down through Sunbury, because if it did it would be inundated two months in the year at least. It could not go * down the western shore of the St. John river, because the gradients would be such as would make it an impossible route. It would have to go back from the river and follow a line parallel to the Canadian Pacific Railway line. The distance by the route that is proposed via Connor's, Edmundston, Woodstock, Fredericton, Chip-man and Norton would be, to St. John, 437 miles. You must go around by Chipman, utilizing the Chipman line and going down over the Intercolonial from Norton to St. John. The distance, as I have said, is 437 miles. I am going to point out the difference between what is known as the Chipman route and the western banks of the St. John river route, which is practically the present route of the Canadian Pacific Railway ; that is by way of Woodstock and McAdam. The distance is 398 miles.
Is that around by McAdam ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It must strike in somewhere near Harvey.
You are using the present route of the Canadian Pacific Railway ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: You would have to go down nearly 60 miles paralleling the Canadian Pacific Railway to St. John. I am giving the exact mileage, but it would depend very largely upon whether the route would end on the present line of the Canadian Pacific Railway at Harvey or Fredericton junction. If at Fredericton junction the distance would not be so great. If at Harvey it would be some miles longer.
What would it be doing at Harvey ? It is not going through the state of Maine.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It would go over from Woodstock.
To Harvey ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is Harvey not in Canada ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Well, then Fredericton juncton would be the junction point. That would be many miles from the boundary line of Maine.	1
Harvey is about half way between McAdam junction and Fredericton junction ?
Would it not be shorter to go down the valley of the St. John river to Fredericton ?	[DOT]

It is exactly 39 miles shorter. If you were to go down the St. John river, you would find yourself on the western bank of the St. John river at Carle-ton port, which is not possible. You would have to get on the eastern banks of the St. John river into the city proper. They have not sufficient room for ships and they have no terminal facilities on the western side of the harbour, and it would be out of the question to attempt to have enlarged terminal facilities on the western side of St. John river harbour, the Canadian Pacific having exclusive advantages there. If you were to attempt to go on the west side, you would only save 39 miles. By going around by Chipman you are within a certain distance of Moncton, and if Canada is to aid a railway, and with that magnificent harbour of Halifax and with the advantages of St. John harbour, because I do not wish to minimize the advantages which St. John possesses, and from the standpoint of Mr. Hays there would be more traffic than any one Mr. EMMERSON.
harbour could handle, I think this route is entitled to consideration. Now, summarizing distances, by way of Chipman down to Boiestown it would be 368 miles to Moncton. By the Nashwaak bridge route it would be precisely, or practically, the same distance to Moncton. The Boiestown route was the route surveyed by Mr. Hartley, an engineer who surveyed that route previous to confederation. The present route of the Intercolonial Railway was known as the Major Robinson route. He surveyed it through the northern section of the province. Mr. Hartley surveyed what is known as the central route right up through the rich valley of the St. John. There is one thing that must not be lost sight of in this matter. I do not think that sectional differences should prevail, but I do say that if Canada is to aid in the construction of a railway on Canadian soil and covering the shortest possible distance, if the railway is constructed by the Chipman route it would open up the best sections of the country. I think I can speak for New Brunswick, having a knowledge of it that few have had the opportunity to possess, and as far as New Brunswick is concerned this route via Chipman will develop and open up one of the best sections of the country that we have, rich in mineral resources and fertile agricultural lands. It would open up and develop a country which to-day, by reason of the want of railway facilities, is lying undeveloped. The mere distance of 37 miles should have no weight when compared with the vast advantages which would accrue from this route. It would be absurd to talk of running a railway to St. John parallel to the present Canadian Pacific Railway, and if the suggestions of some hon. gentlemen were carried out, it would be tantamount to the building of a parallel line. As one of the representatives of New Brunswick, I certainly strongly urge, as I have already strongly urged, the adoption of Moncton as the terminal point in eastern Canada.
Did you say 176 miles ?
I think it is 176 miles from Moncton to Halifax by the present route of the Intercolonial Railway.
One hundred and eighty-five miles.

Very well. It is absurd to talk about going to Moncton and running back over the Intercolonial Railway to St. John, a distance of eighty-nine miles, because if my hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Oliver) would prepare a little map for himself he would at once see how it is possible to get to St. John in a very much easier way by adopting the present Central system and a portion of the Intercolonial Railway. That is the route that the engineers have spoken of, and that is the route which practical railway men have

approved. I have said that the distance from the Cliaudiere to Moncton by either of the central routes would be 30S miles, whereas the distance between the Chaudi&re Junction and Moncton by the present route of the Intercolonial Railway is 497 3-10 miles, showing a saving of 129 3-10 miles. If you go down and parallel the Canadian Pacific Railway following the western banks of the St. John river, far from the banks, and in a country which from my knowledge is not available for easy railway construction, you would only save thirty-seven miles difference as between these two routes. I feel certain that if sectional views were to prevail so far as the province of New Brunswick is concerned, the views of the people who understand the geographical and topographical conditions of the country are practically all in favour of the adoption of the route) via Moucton as against the adoption of the western route paralleling the Canadian Pacific Railway to St. John.
Hear, hear.

If there were any sectional ideas prevailing, I can quite understand that possibly the city of St. John would naturally favour the route on the western side of the St. John river, but St. John is not the whole of the province of New Brunswick and no one need run away with that idea. Whatever may be the views of the citizens of St. John, they are not by auy means the views of the people of the province of ~New Brunswick in this particular at least.
Hear, hear.

Might I ask the hon. geu-tlernan (Mr. Emmerson) if he has considered what effect, if any, the construction of this proposed line will have upon the Intercolonial Railway so far as freight and passenger traffic are concerned ?

I do not fancy that it would have any great, or even any material effect because by reason of the Canadian Pacific Railway route between Montreal and St. John; St. John has the advantage in securing the traffic. But the great traffic which the Intercolonial Railway possesses, is peculiar to itself and one which it must necessarily retain. The Intercolonial Railway skirts the shores of the St. Lawrence; it runs at the head of those rich harbours and bays in northern New Brunswick which are teeming with fish. That traffic will always belong to the Intercolonial Railway. It runs through a rich agricultural country; a country rich in lumber resources as every one knows. That traffic would not meet with any material depreciation. We must of course conclude that the traffic on this new line will be through traffic, and unfortunately the Intercolonial Railway has not possessed that through traffic to any considerable extent. That is another strong
reason why the Intercolonial Railway would not lose that which it never has had.

I would not have addressed the committee were it not that my hon. friend from St. John has made an appeal for his city and spoken of his great faith in it.
The theological definition of faith is :
Faith is the substance of things hoped for ;
The evidence of things not seen.
I prefer in material matters to walk by sight and not by faith. Now, Sir, I do not desire to set up Halifax as a rival of St. John. I do not wish to excite any feelings of emulation even. In the past, when St. John has been mentioned it" has always been supposed that there was a considerable amount of rivalry on the part of Halifax. I shall not take any sectional view of the question at all, but I wish to impress upon the committee the duty of selecting a common place of distribution and that place has been named by many of the speakers to be the common centre of Moncton, through which the lines will radiate to whatever points are available. From Moncton you can go to St. John; you can go to, Pietou; you can go to Halifax; you can go to Sydney; you can go to Country Harbour or any other place. I say that in Nova Scotia and Halifax we have a right to expect a participation in the benefits derived from through freight from any part of the country wliere-ever it may be, and we ask for no more than that. We ask for no monopoly, we ask for no invidious selection of our own port, but we do ask that all may participate and that we shall merely have that share of the trade of the country that nature has destined for us. But I would say that if you would undertake to carry these goods for shipment to the port of St. John you will remember that this is not a terminus. The object of taking these goods to the sea-board is for shipment to Europe, and therefore in that link of ocean navigation when you bring your goods to the harbour of Halifax it balances the difference which may 'be against Halifax in the matter of railroad carriage, because When you come to the port of Halifax in your steamer you have 300 miles to go up the Bay of Fundy to1 St. John, a most difficult bit of navigation in the winter time. St. John is 300 miles further from Europe than is Halifax, and therefore in the in-going and out-going trip you have 600 miles more of most difficult navigation in the winter season, which is the season when these goods will be shipped from a maritime province port, if they are ever carried over this railway. From the knowledge which I have of this matter, I can say that these 600 miles of difficult navigation for these large steamers is a balance over expenses if you carried the freight twice between Moncton and

Halifax to ship from that port. I think it would be much cheaper to ship from Halifax than from St. John, although St. John may be a few miles nearer on the railway.

Having furnished the House with some figures, possibly it would be fair if*I gave the details on which those figures were based. This information was obtained by me in the Railway Department. From Chaudiere to Edinundston in the county of Madawaska, New Brunswick, the distance is 1G2 miles. From Edinundston to Plaster Eock, on the Tobique river, by way of St. Leonards, the distance is 48 miles. From Plaster Eock to Boiestown, the distance is 55 miles. From Boiestown to Moncton by way of Berry's Mills the distance is 75 miles. The totals 340 miles. 276 of the mileage, is unsurveyed country. The rule of engineers is to add 10 per cent for curves. Therefore, adding 28 miles to the 340 miles makes 368 miles. The Nasli-waak Bridge route is somewhat nearer Fredericton than the Boiestown route. From Chaudiere to St. John via Fredericton on the left or western side of the river, the distances, are : from Chaudiere to Edmund-ston, 162 miles ; from Edmundston to Fredericton, 170 miles by the Canadian Pacific Railway mileage ; and from Fredericton to St. John, 66 miles, by the present route of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I think probably on account of gradings this route would be somewhat lengthened. The total mileage of the last route is 398 miles as against 437 miles by way of Cliipman to Norton, on the Intercolonial Railway, and back to the Canadian Pacific Railway, lauding you on the eastern bank of the St. John harbour.
What is the distance from Chaudiere to St. John by way of Woodstock and Harvey ?
I took it by Fredericton Junction. I give that as 39S miles.

I did not propose nor do I propose to take any part in the discussion so far as it appears to be a question between the relative claims of Halifax, St. John and Moncton. I think that partakes too much of a sectional character to interest this committee, and I am sure that we are not contributing to the estimation in which we would like to be held in this House by entering upon those controversies under the circumstances as they exist to-night. When this Bill was before the Railway Committee, I did not offer any objection to the strongly expressed desire of the members, chiefly from Nova Scotia, and one at least from New Brunswick, that Moncton should be made the terminus of this new line, and I will tell you why I did not. Not because I did not feel that it was a very important question ; not because I did not feel that there were very grave reasons why it would Mr. ROCHE (Halifax).
not be to the interest of Canada from a national point of view that that question should be settled ; but because I was satisfied in my own mind that that was not the place or^tlie occasion on which a question of that kind should be settled. Nor do I think that to-night or this committee is the time or the place when a question of this kind can be properly determined. This committee can accept neither the statement made by my hon. friend from Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) nor the statement of my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan) as to the distances between the points mentioned, or as to the best routes to select between Chaudiere and the ocean. We are not possessed of the information necessary to enable us to decide those questions. No surveys have teen made ; no one can say what circuitous route might have to be taken in order to place the terminus of this line at Moncton ; and this committee would not be safely guided by acting on such representations, though made in good faith, and in every confidence that they are correct, in the absence of sufficient data. This committee would not be wise in being guided to a definite conclusion without further information on those points. I am not disposed, then, to engage in any controversy on this question, but I leave it for the present where my hon. friends have left it, and I make bold to say that whefi this question comes to be finally determined, no government is strong enough to determine it other than in the true national interests of Canada. When this question comes to be determined, it will be determined only after there has been a complete and thorough survey of the whole ground. If it comes to be necessary in the interest of Canada as a whole, to build another competing line with the Intercolonial Railway, for which I do not see any necessity at the present time, the government must be sure that it founds its conclusions on evidence that will be complete, conclusive and satisfactory as to the proper route to select. While I will not take any part in this controversy, I feel bound to say to my hon. friends who have cast reflection on either the capacity or the efficiency or the national character of the port of St. John, that they have not been warranted in the statements they have made, and I am sorry my hon. friends have taken this occasion to make' these reflections. My hon. friend from Cumberland spoke of the tricky tides of the Bay of Fundy. I want to know what is the data oh which my hon. friend considers himself justified in so characterizing that great waterway. Let him take up the returns made from time to time, reliable returns, and see -what is the nature of the casualties which have occurred in that bay, and I venture to say that there is no bay on the whole northern coast of this continent which has been so free from accidents,

so free from casualties, and so safe to navigate as the Bay of Fundy. I am not going to make any reflections on the harbour of Halifax. I do not know that I could do it, but I would not do it if I could, because it is not a question which ought to he raised in this manner before this committee, and holding the opinion I do, I would not raise it if I were ever so much in position to do so.
Another hon. gentleman has talked about the small size of the harbour and its lack of capacity to handle traffic. No one who knows anything about St. John would make that statement. It is quite true that there has been a congestion of traffic in that port. But why ? Because the harbour has been dependent almost entirely on the expenditures made by the people of St. John themselves to provide traffic facilities. But we have plenty of room to provide additional accommodation. There is no end to the amount of business which can be done, but there is a limit to the capacity of the people to put their hands into their pockets and provide facilities, and it is because the people have not been able to provide traffic facilities in a greater measure that the complaint is made concerning congestion of shipping. I do not know where my hon. friend gets his measurements. He says it is 300 miles more or less from Europe further to the port of St. John than to the port of Halifax. I am amazed to hear such a statement. If I could cross the Bay of Fundy on boat and go to Halifax, it would not be more than 120 to 130 miles at the most in a direct line. We do not propose to take those steamers over the land, but my hon. friend has forgotten that it is not going to be necessary, in the interests of the business of Canada, for a steamer loading at the port of St. John for Europe to go all the way round the coast of Nova Scotia until she comes to the harbour of Halifax. She will put right out and get across in less than half the distance which my hon. friend says has to be traversed more to reach the port of St. John than I-Ialfax. But there is no doubt whatever on this point, that the harbour of St. John is accessible, is free from ice, is in every respect a safe harbour and is capable of expansion to any degree which the business of the country will require for some time to come, and when the question comes to be considered commercially, it will not be found necessary to decide it in the way some hon. gentlemen propose who have expressed their opinions here to-night.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I think that this discussion is out of place and untimely, but when it comes to be a question of comparison between the merits of the harbour of St. John and those of Halifax, I cannot refrain from taking a part in the discussion. After this charter is granted and the government decide to assist the company, it will be time to say what route
should be adopted. No person of sound mind would for a moment think of comparing Halifax to St. John. You can spend millions of dollars on St. John and you will never make it but a small mud hole in comparison with Halifax. It is only the other day that a big steamer was wrecked in the harbour itself, because it had not room to turn around and get to its proper mooring. The harbour of Halifax has been claimed by the best navigators who ever frequented the ports of North America, to be equal to any in the world except that of Rio in South America and Sydney in New South Wales. You come in from the sea and in half an hour you are into a safe, commodious harbour, with an ordinary rise and fall of from four and a half feet and in spring tides six feet. You get your load and go away, and in half an hour are out on the ocean. You have a clear course to go wherever you want, whereas in the harbour of St. John you have a thirty feet rise and fall of the tide, and when that tide is out, it is not a very desirable place for steamers to go to. If that port is to be the terminus of this road, it would be better that this road were never built.

Referring to what my hon. friend who has just spoken has said regarding St. John harbour, I would like to say a few words. The harbour of St. John has had some of the largest men-of-war-the great standard of Halifax-in it and they lay there with perfect safety. I agree with my hon. friend that Halifax harbour, when you get into it, is all right, but he can give no instance in the port of St. John and that so-called terrible place the Bay of Fundy, of a number of lives or vessels lost, although the tonnage and the shipping going to that port has far exceeded that in the port of Halifax. This has strengthened the hands of the merchants and underwriters. What is the matter with the St. Lawrence, with its insurance rates unusually high and a number of ships constantly going ashore ? I see sometimes in reading the papers, that as many as four ships have gone ashore in the one day. But you do not find anything of that kind in the port of St. John. Ships move in and out with perfect safety, and they have nothing at all to interfere with them. We have plenty of tide but not more than Bristol.
The ships must anchor outside until the tide rises.

Not at all, they can come in at all times, and thanks to the government, the present bar is to be removed. That will be done as soon as a dredge is built for that purpose. The world was not made in a day. Six years ago there was no grain shipped from the port of St. John, but the people living there had such confidence in the capabilities of that port that

they put their hands into their pockets and spent $750,000 in the construction of the present wharfs and gave for the use of the Canadian Pacific Railway, to assist their coming into our-port, property which, in the books of that company, is valued at a million dollars. The progress of St. John within the last six years has been simply wonderful. I feel sure that for every hundred bushels shipped from St. John, not more than one is shipped from Halifax. Such is the difference between the two ports, and the port of Halifax was amply assisted by the late government. Elevators and wharfs were built, and railways were brought down into the city and everything that could be done was done for the young child, but it did nothing for the good of the country. The merchants of our country and farmers are not shipping their produce to Great Britain from Halifax, and I doubt whether they will do so in the future.

It is very much to be regretted that this discussion should have been provoked by the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver). The question was before the committee and thoroughly discussed the other day, and a test vote taken, which resulted in the Bill being reported to the House in the form in which it now stands. All hon. gentlemen are aware that when this Bill was presented to the House the eastern terminus named was the city of Quebec. The maritime province members almost to a man joined together before the committee in urging that Moncton should be the eastern terminus of the road for the present. The discussion took place In the presence of the promoters of the Bill, the authorities of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and that discussion seemed to convince them that Moncton was the proper place for them to have for their eastern terminus. And they, of their own motion amended the Bill and presented it to the House in that form. After long and careful* discussion, this was adopted by the Railway Committee, and the Bill was so reported to the House. Now, it does seem to me unfortunate that the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) should provoke a discussion here to-night which can result in no good, for there is no resolution before the committee, merely for the purpose of airing his views as to what is best for the maritime provinces. I believe that all the representatives for Nova Scotia, and I think the members from Prince Edward Island also, and nearly every member from the province of New Brunswick, are in a better position to judge what is best for the eastern end of the Dominion than is my hon. friend from the west.
