If we were to attempt to interfere with his territory in the slightest degree we should hear from him, and I think we may well ask him to allow us to manage our own affairs in this direction. The hon. gentleman's argument is that this Mr. TUCKER.
will not be a national railway, because Moncton is not a port. Nobody ever contended that it was. The hon. gentleman is reviving once more the old discussion about Halifax and St. John. The relative merits of St. John and Halifax have been gone over on the floor of this House and in every part of the eastern half of the Dominion until every one is tired and sick of the subject. And one reason why we have never accomplished anything in the lower provinces is that as soon as anything is proposed to be done, this controversy is provoked, it neutralizes the efforts of those who seek to accomplish something and so nothing is gained. When we met and agreed upon Mo acton as the objective point, we thought we had got rid of this discussion; and I believe we had until the hon. gentleman brought it up again. The position taken 'by the maritime provinces is this, and I think it was fair-first, we recognized that the west must be developed and the duty devolves upon the government of providing increased facilities for the removal of its products. We do not say to the west : We wish to compel your products to come to a maritime province port, or that we are going to control your route of freight in any way or to ask you a fraction of a cent more on freight for your goods than if they were going by any other way; but we will leave you to ship your goods in any way youi see fit so as to get to your market in the cheapest possible way. But we have a right to say further, and we do say : If this Dominion is to spend an enormous amount of money for the purpose of developing the west, we in the maritime provinces have a right to a share of that expenditure; we have a right to see to it that our interests are guarded as well as those in the west. If we are willing to concede everything to them and take the position that we do not wish to injure them, we think we are right in making the demand wre are making and that we are going to stand for, namely the extension of this road to Moncton if the roadl is to be aided by the government. It is stated that the Intercolonial Railway was built for the benefit of the maritime provinces, and that is one of the things that it is very hard for a Nova Scotian to stand. The Intercolonial Railway was not built for us, and accomplished no good for us. We were not the people who were sought to be benefited by it. It was located around by the north shore of New Brunswick. Why ? Some said it was so located for military purposes, and some that it was to enhance the value of the property of some individual. Whatever may have been the object, the results were the same to us. The Intercolonial Railway has accomplished no good for us, on the contrary, it has been a vast injury and a hindrance to our progress. Why ? Because it enabled the merchants and manufacturers of Montreal, Toronto and other centres in the old Cana-

das to come down with their products and compete with our manufacturers and drive out of business nearly all our wholesale merchants. They have had the use of the Intercolonial Railway, they have had the cheap rates, we have not had the benefit of these rates, because we have nothing to ship that the older provinces are willing to take from us. And, so far as the farmers of Nova Scotia are concerned, the products of Ontario and the west come down and compete with our products to the injury of our Nova Scotia farmers. It is true, we get cheap rates on coal, but how far west can we send coal ? We do not get it farther west than Montreal, and we could send it to that port by water even if the Intercolonial had never been built. We have been injured by this line and it took us twenty-five years to adapt ourselves to the position we were placed in by the building of that road. 1 When the Canadian Pacific Railway was built, we were then promised a shoi't line of railway across the province of New Brunswick to Salisbury near Moncton. That was taken from us, and the road was built across the state of Maine to the city of St. John, receiving government aid, and we were left without any connection in that direction. And now comes this project -to build another transcontinental road ; and we say that if it is to be carried through with government aid, we put forward our claims, and we deny that the fact of the construction of the Intercolonial Railway should) be quoted against us. We want *a short line from Moncton to Oliaudiere, and we are entitled to it. We have agreed to that, so far as we are concerned. When we get to Moncton we are on the Inter- { colonial and have a direct line to the city of Halifax. I am sorry that any bon. gentleman here has seen fit to say anything against either great port. That is unwise.
I believe it is better for us to praise our country rather than to decry it. I am willing to agree to everything the hon. gentleman from St. John has said with regard to his harbour. It is true they can ship a great deal of grain from there. I am willing to agree to everything he said and also to go further and to say that within the last few weeks it has given promise of being a great game preserve, for we have had moose wandering around it. I do not say that in any unpleasant way, or as detracting from the merits of St. John harbour.
I know what they can do there in the way of handling freight. The new road, however, can not be brought in upon the western side of St. John harbour, for all tlio available space there is occupied by the Canadian Pacific Railway. They must come in on the eastern side, and, to do that, they must come down by way of Chipmun upon the line we have indicated.
I do not know that it is necessary for me to refer at any length to the subject of national spirit and the building up of a natioual highway, these are good terms, and I like to hear them. But the national highway that we want is the one that will serve the whole Dominion. If the west want an outlet for the product of the west on merely commercial basis you should not lay a single rail east of Winnipeg, but should divert the traffic by way of the United States. Are we prepared to do that ?	1
believe we are not. I believe we are prepared, as a Dominion, to make sacrifices in order to prevent that being done. We are willing to say to the west that we want to make this a continuing Dominion, to prevent the Dominion breaking up in the future when the interests have changed from what they are now. For that reason we have urged strongly, and will urge strongly, that the terminus of this road shall be at Moncton. And I appeal to the fair-play and spirit of justice of the hon. members if the provinces of Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick are not entitled to some consideration. There is no talk of any injury to St. John if they get there. If this road with an increased cjjstance of thirty-seven miles over a direct line, gets to St. John, I do not think the city of St. John has anything to complain of. While I am on my feet, let me give expression to what my views are on the subject.
1 believe that the freight going over this road will in the natural course of events, gravitate to St. John ; I believe just as firmly that the passenger traffic and the mails must go through Halifax. If a fast line service is ever constructed for the Dominion of Canada it must run from the port of Halifax. When you have those things, and when in addition you have the port of Quebec properly equipped with a perfect freight service there, and the port of Montreal properly equipped, and the St. Lawrence river properly equipped, and dredged, and put in proper condition, then you are in the best position to take care of the freight that is coming from the west. It is madness for us to suppose that we can be able to divert the whole traffic from the port of Portland. If the officers of the Grand Trunk Railway Company came before this committee to-night and said that it was their intention to pull up their terminus at Portland, I could not credit it, because they need this terminus in order to take care of their business. We cannot compel them to leave Portland, and I don't think we should ask them to do it ; I doubt if it would be in the interest of the western country for them to do it. But when we are providing this road, we should provide that as much freight as possible should go through Canadian channels and be shipped from Canadian ports. Let us lay no stress upon shipping, either in or out. Now we are labouring under some disadvantages. Let me tell hon. gentlemen of the anomalous position that exists with regard to the freight from the maritime pro-

vinces going west. A gentleman told me the other day that he had a certain class of heavy freight to ship from Halifax to Toronto, and he found that he could ship it cheaper from Halifax to Liverpool and back to Ontario as through freight, and save money by the transaction. That is how we are circumstanced with regard to these freights. We are simply asking for justice for the lower provinces. I regret that the question of rival ports has been brought up. There was no necessity for it, because the company themselves say they are willing to go down to Moncton. They have put that in their Bill, and why should we try to disturb it. The hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) talks about an increase of distance of 176 miles to Halifax. Nobody is talking about tnking freight to Halifax. Let the freight go to St. John if it will.
Why would you go a longer way round when you can reach your objective point much shorter, and at the same time compete more successfully with cheaper lines ?

I will answer the hon. gentleman by saying to him that we do n(ft propose to do anything of the sort. W'e do not propose to go by a longer line. The route they would be compelled to take in order to get from the western side of the harbour of St. John will be thirty-seven miles longer than if they went by Chipman to the eastern side, and if St. John can be put in that position surely they have the right to raise this sectional cry. I deprecate it, I am sorry it has been made. We are agreed upon a given point, and I thought we had buried for ever this senseless war that has existed between Halifax and St. John for years and years, and which is paralyzing the efforts of the representatives of the two provinces in this parliament whenever we attempt to do anything for the two provinces. I appeal to them now to let this matter drop. Let us go forward, having agreed upon the neutral point, and then let the traffic and the travel go from there where it will. If it goes to St. John from Chipman, let St. John have it; if the travel goes to Halifax, that is the proper place for it to go to. We must meet upon common ground, and we must yield in these matters. If we cannot get everything we want in this world we must be satisfied to take what we can get. bearing in mind that there are others in the world beside ourselves.

I have been delighted with the remarks of the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade). They have the right ring. I think a maritime province man should be big enough to say : Let any port in the maritime province win in the game ; bring your route to the maritime provinces and let God and nature determine the port. People are easily caught by catch

phrases. Start a catch phrase up in this country and it takes away all the argument you can make in a year. One hon. gentleman deprecates paralleling the Intercolonial. Why, we want railways in this country paralleling every eight or ten miles. Parallel railways every eight or ten miles and you bring in population, you bring in industry, and you produce wealth. I had an opportunity the other day to discuss this question of parallel lines. I found in the great states of Ohio and Illinois that they have paralleled railways to a wonderful extent. The state of Illinois has about
60,000	square miles, and they have between 14,000 and 15,000 miles of railway packed into that 60,000 square miles, while the whole of Canada has barely 18,000 miles. Well, you never heard the people of Ohio complain about their lines being parallel.
An lion. MEMBER. Who built tlieir lines?

That is not part of my argument at the present time. I want 1o show that just as you parallel lines and build them close together, you develop the country, you get an enormous population, and you get great empire states. Now Ohio has 14,000 miles of railway, with a population of nearly 5,000,000, almost ns many people as exist in the whole Dominion of Canada. Why ? Because they have paralleled the whole state with railways and enabled five millions of people to live in that state, and to develop the business and Wealth of that country. The great trouble with Canada is that notwithstanding our enormous resources we cannot get the country developed, and therefore we cannot have population. I think we should imitate the state of Illinois in this respect, with its .14,000 miles of railway in 60,000 square miles of territory. Why, Sir, the province of Ontario, with 256,000 square miles of territory, has no more than 4,000 or 5,000 miles of railway. You people of Ontario ought to be ashamed talking about keeping railways apart, you have not got any railways in the province of Ontario. Still I am bound to say that you people of Ontario have got more railways than we have in the province of Nova Scotia. We are uncivilized in Nova Scotia, we are uncivilized in New Brunswick, because we have got no railways. A railway to-day is a great civilizer. We have got clergymen in our province, they are civilizers, but we have not got railways. Now, I want to see the Intercolonial paralleled, for the very instant you parallel it, you will have what has occurred in Ohio. Just in proportion as the railways of Ohio were paralleled the value of stocks increased. Twenty or thirty years ago when the railways of Ohio were few and far between, the stocks were scarcely of any value, now they are all first-class, and every railroad to-day is paying dividends in the state of Ohio.
Are these railways all confined to the limits of the state of Ohio ?
I am talking about the number of railways in the state of Ohio.
How can you say they paid dividends in the state of Ohio ?

I say that so far as the railways in Ohio are concerned, the abundance of traffic enables them to pay their way. Now then let me say another thing in reference to the state of Illinois which is the great middle state of the west. That state has something like 53,000 square miles. It has about 13,000 miles of railway and there are almost 5,000,000 people in it. These two states, Ohio and Illinois, have
27,000	or 28,000 miles of railway, almost double the mileage of railways in Canada, and they have only about one half the territory of the province of Ontario. Now then I want to bring this home so that our people will stop this infernal nonsense of talking about paralleling railways. We want to parallel our railways every ten miles before we can take our position as a country of progress and enterprise. When we get the Intercolonial Railway paralleled every ten miles through New Brunswick, I will undertake to say that hon. gentlemen will not have a word to say about the Intercolonial Railway paying or not paying, because the construction of parallel railways will give a stimulus to the enterprise of that province. It is a barren province to-day. The whole interior of the country has to be opened up and you cannot have progress without railways. A man will not go iOO miles from a railway, invest his money and undertake to do business. You must have railways. The great modern civilizer is the railway. I am going to ask this House to give us some bonuses in the county of Colchester. You may think that because we have sea routes we are necessarily in a position to dispense with railways. The contrary is the fact. There is another thing that I want to mention. In Germany and on the continent of Europe where they have great canals, it has been found that wherever there was a canal running from one city to another it would not pay, but wherever that canal was paralleled by a railway, both paid. The railway helped the canal and the canal helped the railway. You will find that in the report that was issued by the Senate which took the testimony of the most competent men on this continent in reference to transportation. If I propounded that to the wise men of this House they would say it is impossible, and yet competent men came before a committee of the Senate and showed that in Germany canals that had not paid, on being paralleled by railways were found to pay. What was the explanation ? The explanation was that the canal carried the heavy freight which was not a paying freight to the railway, while the railway carried the light freight which was not a source of profit on the canal. Consequently, both paid. You want a railway to be paralleled every five or ten miles and the parallel lines will pay. I do not want to hear any more of that nonsense that we hear in the Railway Committee, and all over the country, about paralleling railways. We want railways to be paralleled every ten miles. I want hon. gentlemen to look into the statistics of Ohio and Illinois. They afford magnificent food for any one who takes the trouble to look into this question of railway building. Ohio and Illinois are the wealthiest states in the union, barring the state of New York. In these great states manufacturing and agriculture have reached a high point, and the reason is that both manufacturers and farmers find themselves near railways. The farmers do not have to carry their grain thirty or forty miles to a railway as in our country. We compel farmers in this country to cart their grain thirty or forty miles to a railway and expect them to make money. I was ashamed this summer when you asked those immigrants to come out to this country, because, instead of having railways to enable them to ship their first crop to the markets of the world, you had them dumped down 300 or 400 miles from a railroad and you expect to maintain the reputation of Canada under circumstances of that kind. Some hon. gentlemen in the committee have spoken of Halifax as being far away. Halifax is a port which will beat Portland in distance and it will secure the business if the people of Canada understand the problem and appreciate the advantages which they possess. WTe want air lines with heavy rails, big cars and no gradients. Then we will have the same conditions as those which exist in the United States. There it is found that railways will give you the advantage of a long haul. AVith these heavy rails and big cars they will haul your grain 2,500 miles for exactly the same rate as that which they will haul it for 2,000 miles or less. The long haul cuts down the distance, and under similar conditions in this country 200 or 300 miles will make no difference. The railways will deliver freights at the same rate at Halifax as at Quebec. This is the question and this is the problem that has been worked out in the United States, and if it had been otherwise no state in the west, such as Nebraska, could possibly compete with a state farther east. In this country we talk about making a national port and it is said that Portland is 100 miles nearer than Halifax. The man who makes that statement does not do any credit to his head or his heart. I was glad that the hon. member for Annapolis made the point that he did make. I am persuaded, while I have no sectional or unkind word to say about any part of Canada, that the Intercolonial Railway has been a better commercial investment to the people of Ontario than it has been to the people of the maritime provinces.

Ml-. McCarthy. Mr. Chairman, I desire to rise to a point of order. I would not with ali respect try to stop my hon. friend's eloquence, but he has given notice of a motion that he intends to move which is in amendment to the clause which is now under discussion. I understand the address which he is delivering is in criticism of the clause as it now exists. To strike out the whole clause would not be in order. No motion is before you to strike out the clause and the discussion is upon the question whether the clause will be adopted or not. As has already been said, it is in the nature of an agreement whereby Moncton was named as the terminus, and that agreement has not been sought to be set aside. I assume then that the hon. gentleman should confine this discussion properly to this clause.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Gourley) is extending beyond the clause. Of course, he is not discussing the notice of motion, because he simply read it and handed it to the clerk. I hope hon. members who are discussing this clause will confine themselves to it.

I think my hon. friend (Mr. Gourley) is perfectly in order. Some remarks have been made by the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) against the scope of this clause and the remarks of the hou. member for Colchester are in support of the clause as it stands. It may be he wants something further added to it, but he is arguing in favour of the clause to that extent.
Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER, I did not say the hon. gentleman was out of order, but I gave a warning to the committee to keep as closely as possible to the consideration of the clause.

I do not want to have to argue that the Intercolonial Railway is a disadvantage to Nova Scotia or an advantage to Ontario, but I want the people of Ontario to understand that we in Nova Scotia regard it more as a national necessity in favour of Ontario than in favour of Nova Scotia. I undertake to say that the people of Ontario get Infinitely more out of the investment in the Intercolonial Railway than do the people of Nova Scotia. We are not a manufacturing people ; we buy your products and we have nothing to send you in return, except it be coal. I do not like a discussion on this line, because I think that our policy should be a policy for all Canada and not for any province or provinces. The Intercolonial Railway was a political necessity, just as the Canadian Pacific Railway was a national necessity, and fortunately both of these enterprises will in time turn out to be great commei-cial successes. If this great railway system is to be brought to the maritime provinces, I want that it shall be so hedged that the point of export Mr. GOURLEY.
will be in the maritime provinces and not at Portland. This is the most important debate in this parliament since I have been a member, because it points to a broadening of the national life of our country. While this country sends its goods to a foreign port for shipment we never can have a national sentiment, and this debate is worth a dozen debates on tupenny-hapenny subjects which it never would make a difference whether decided one way or the other. This is a national debate calculated to give national ideas to the people of Canada, and to direct their attention towards looking at Canada as a whole. If the debate has promoted that feeling, it will have advanced the interests of Canada in an immeasurable degree.

This clause was discussed for several days in the committee, and one day the maritime province members got together and reached the conclusion that they would be perfectly satisfied if the terminus of this road was fixed at Moncton. While this discussion may be very interesting, I do not know that it is of any benefit to Canada. We heard to-night the hon. member for Victoria (Hon. Mr. Ross), an exmember of the Liberal government, telling us that the port of St. John was a mud hole, that no sane man would ever advocate it as a terminus, and that if St. John were to be the terminus, then the road had better never be built. It is detrimental to the interests of this country that a man occupying the prominent position of the member for Victoria should state in this parliament that one of our principal seaports is a mud hole.
The member for what Victoria ?

Victoria, N.S. On the other hand, we have had hon. members to get up and tell us that Halifax is not suitable. Now, Sir, under clause 12 of this Bill the company is simply given the right to build a certain line of railway. There is nothing to compel the company to build any particular section of that road, and whether they build it or not, it is entirely permissive. We want to know what the government policy is in regard to this road, and we have a right to know it. Time and again in the committee it was asked that the government should announce their policy in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific, so that we might discuss the Bill intelligently. It may be that the government do not intend to give one dollar of subsidy to the Grand Trunk Pacific ; and if that be the ease, then we know from those who are promoting the Bill that they will not build a mile of the railway. It may be that the government intend to subsidize that portion from Quebec westward, or it may be from Moncton westward, but whatever their policy be, until the announcement of it is made to the House, it is waste of time for us to discuss the Bill.

It seems to me that the proper course to pursue is to let this Bill go on, and when the government announces its policy then we can better know" what we are doing in respect to this measure.

If I believed that this discussion was profitless I would show the strength of my conviction by not taking part in it. I do not take that view, however, ancTin fact the discussion so far has brought out in one instance such very remarkable propositions that it is just as well to make allusion to them. If I viewed the matter as does the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) I would not have raised this discussion to-night, but I do not view it in that way and I hope the House and the country do not view it in that way. That hon. gentleman set forth the idea, that so far as the members from the maritime provinces were concerned they were prepared to let the North-west get out its grain in any way it liked but they demanded their share of the general expenditure. It was a matter of expenditure to them, and not a matter of transportation. If that is their point of view, it is no wonder that they demand that the railway shall go to a place that is not a port rather than to a nearer place that is a port. It is of course a pity that any section of the members of this House by acting together cannot provide a policy for the House and the country-it is a pity, possibly, from their point of view. But I humbly submit that the people whose exertions will furnish the traffic for the railroad are more interested in the length of the railroad, the location of the railroad, and the terminus of the railroad, than any other set of men in the country; because they will pay their share towards building the railroad, and after it is built they will be the people who will keep it going. Whether they live in the west or in the east, the people who are expected to furnish the traffic of the railroad are the people who should have some say as to the length of the railway, the cost of the haul, and the terminus of the railway. They do not get together in a caucus in order to force any policy on the House and the country. They have taken for granted that this would be treated as a national matter, and that justice would be done in the premises. It seems that this is not to be the case, but that the road is to be lengthened, it may be ninety-five miles or it may 185 miles; but it is to be lengthened, because it has been so decided by gentlemen who represent provinces into which the railroad will not run. This is the proposition which is placed before the House and the country; I hope the hon. gentlemen who support it are proud of their position. I do not endorse it, and I would not like to be thought guilty of supporting such a proposition. Let me ask the hon. gentleman who said that the Intercolonial was an injury to the maritime provinces, if that is so, why, in heaven's name, does he want another road built to the maritime provinces 3 Surely, it would be better to tear up the rails of the Intercolonial than to ask for another railway to be built there. I never before heard such a statement made in this House in regard to a national question. Let me tell the House that to-day the town of Edmonton, which is the jumping off place in the North-west Territories, is using, in the town waterworks, boilers and engines from the Robb Engineering Works, of Amherst, Nova Scotia. There is trade to be done between the west and the east, and the maritime provinces are interested in having the best possible transportation facilities, and it is no more to the best interests of the maritime provinces, nor any section of them that this national railway should be lengthened one mile, than it is to the interests of the people of the North-west or any other part of Canada. If there has been trouble between Halifax and St. John in the past, I certainly would be glad to see it cease. I believe that because of those differences in the past the port of Portland lias had the benefit, and if this suggestion, which has been made ostensibly on behalf of the maritime provinces, is carried out, the port of Portland will continue to have the benefit. An hon. gentleman has spoken of this arrangement as a compromise, if you please, between Halifax and St. John. I have heard of the compromise between the old man and his wife. There were always quarreling as to how the blankets should be divided, and at last there was a compromise and the old lady took the blankets. It appears to me that is about the nature of this compromise. Halifax and St. John have compromised by providing that the railroad shall run some 100 miles distant from St. John. I have been convinced by the facts stated by the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) that there is merit in the proposition to run this proposed line to Chipman, in New Brunswick. His figures are so carefully calculated and his facts so clearly set forth that there can be no doubt about it. The House will understand that it does not make a particle of difference to the argument I have taken the liberty of putting forward how the railroad shall get to St. John. The point is that it shall get to St. John by the shortest possible route. By whatever route it reaches St. John, it will be shorter than a route to any other practicable ocean port in Canada. The hon. gentleman says that if the road is built by way of Chipman to Moncton it will only be within fifty miles of St. John. Then my suggestion is that if there is to be a compromise, and if we are to do away with all this difficulty that has existed between the different sections of the maritime provinces, as well as the difficulty that has probably arisen between the maritime provinces and other

sections of the Dominion, let it be provided that the Grand Trunk shall run that little fifty miles from Chipman to St. John. Surely that is a fairer compromise for everybody and better for the whole country than the proposal that it should run from Chipman to Moncton, from which point the freight would have to be carried 185 miles further to get to Halifax, or 95 miles back to get to St. John.

I do not rise to discuss the merits of the question so much as to challenge a statement or two which fell from the lips of my hon. friend from Annapolis <Mr. Wade) and which I do not think should go without being challenged. The hon. gentleman said that the Intercolonial Railway had not been of any use to the people of the maritime provinces, that it would have been better for them had that road not been built. He stated that after the Intercolonial had been built, the manufacturers and merchants of the west went to the maritime provinces and closed out their manufacturers and merchants. Previous to the building of the Intercolonial Railway, so far as I am informed, the manufactures which the people of the maritime provinces used, which they did not themselves manufacture, came largely from the United States. The manufactures which came from the provinces of Ontario and Quebec replaced those from the United States. If the hon. gentleman will consider the matter further, I think he will see that he did not pay a very great compliment to the manufacturers and merchants of the maritime provinces who, so far as my knowledge of them goes, are shrewd men, and quite competent to compete with those from Quebec and Ontario, when the conditions are equal. When the hon. gentleman says that the west sends everything to the maritime provinces and the maritime provinces sends nothing to the west, he is very much in error. The products of Sydney, New Glasgow, Yarmouth, St. John, Moncton, Halifax, Amherst, and other centres of the maritime provinces are to be found in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario and the North-west, and some of the finest industries this country possesses are to be found in those maritime cities. I rose merely to challenge the statements which the hon. gentleman made. I think that the Intercolonial Railway was a necessity of confederation, and I believe that it has operated to the mutual advantage of the people of the east and the west, and certainly we must all admit that an interprovincial trade is much preferable to a trade between this country and the United States.

I rise merely to correct a misapprehension of some remark I made regarding the harbour of St. John. I do not wish to be understood as having any way depreciated the capacity of that harbour. What I had in my mind-which possibly I may not have expressed as clearly Mr. OLIVER.
as I should-was the fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway have exclusive privileges- and I use the word advisedly and in its broadest sense-on the western side of the harbour, and that it would be necessary for the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway to provide terminal facilities on the eastern side of the harbour. It would therefore be very much more to the advantage to the Grand Trunk Railway to go around even thirty-seven miles more by way of Chipman in order to reach that point than to go down the valley of St. John, paralleling the Canadian Pacific Railway, and reaching only the western side of the harbour. St. John has a splendid harbour and great room for expansion, and I certainly deprecate the references made to the respective advantages or disadvantages of Halifax and St. Jolio. As the hon. member for Annapolis has remarked, the Intercolonial Railway has been somewhat of a disadvantage to the province of Nova Scotia, but I do not think he wished to include the whole of the maritime provinces when he made that remark, because he stated that it was the influence of northern New Brunswick which very largely controlled the location of that road. On a former occasion I referred to the advantage which the Intercolonial Railway has been in cementing old Canada with the maritime provinces, and I will not further refer to that subject. In conclusion, it seems to me that this route, with its thirty-seven miles to Moncton, in addition to what it might be to St. John, is one that will meet the interests, not merely of the maritime provinces, but of Canada as a whole.

I agree with my hon. friend in regretting that any reflection should be cast upon either the harbour of Halifax or St. John. So far as St. John is concerned, I myself, a year ago last December, saw five ocean steamers loading there at one time. That would be sufficient to dissipate any idea that the harbour is not capable of being made the winter port or one of the winter ports of Canada. At the same time I do not want it to be said that I agree with some hon. gentlemen who seem to think that the harbout of Halifax is not fitted to be the winter port or one of the winter ports of this country. The advantages of that harbour have been stated fully by a number of hon. gentlemen so that I need not repeat what they have said. I shall confine myself to stating that there is no port on this side of the Atlantic which is better, and I do not know one that is as good. In addition I can tell my hon. friend from Alberta that some ten or twelve years ago Halifax took more trade from Ontario and the west than it had steamers to accommodate.
I did not make any insinuation against the port of Halifax.

I know that the hon. gentleman is too broad-minded to do

anything of the kind, but I think a number of hon. gentlemen to-night were unduly exercised about some jealousy between the two ports. Let me assure the House that among the business men of Halifax there is no jealousy of St. John. On the contrary they would like to see it prosper. While they would like to see their own port become the winter port, they would prefer that St. John should have this advantage rather than an American port, and I am confident that a similar sentiment prevails among the business men of St. John with regard to Halifax. The business men in both cities are ready to support any project which will make either the winter port of Canada to the exclusion of any foreign harbour, and I do not think that my hon. friend from Alberta exactly understood the purport of the remarks of the hon. member for Annapolis having reference to the expenditure. I was listening with a great deal of attention to the remarks of my hon. friend from Annapolis, and while he used the word ' expenditure,' I understood his remark to mean that the people of the maritime provinces-if you are going to spend much more on the transcontinental-want to share the benefits of that expenditure in the way of transportation facilities. That is the view which my hon. friend from Annapolis presented to the House. The question presents itself to us in this way. Suppose that we built the transcontinental and that it should be diverted 200 miles on this side of Edmonton to Portland in the United States, and thus cut off from Edmonton and its vicinity the benefits of this railway, what they would otherwise enjoy, I think that my hon. friend from Alberta would have something to say if he were not going to get any transportation facilities. The people of the maritime provinces have to look at it in this way. If we are to have another great transcontinental railway, it should have its winter port in this country. In the maritime provinces only can you find a winter port, and they are naturally anxious that the trade should not be diverted to any other country but should be, as far as the commercial conditions warrant, extended to some/ open port in the maritime provinces.
I know that the hon. member for Alberta has expressed himself frankly in favour of that policy to-night and his only objection had regard to the additional length of this line in its extension to St. John. I only make this remark to give to him the benefit of the view which suggests itself, and not unnaturally, to some gentlemen of the maritime provinces. As the promoters have seen fit to assent to Moncton and as there will be no difficulty whatever I suppose to their obtaining additional power to extend from Chipman to St. John, we might leave the matter as at present and indulge in future discussion at some other time, should the government see fit to bring down a measure and ask the House to consent to it.

I wish to correct a statement made, both in the Railway Committee and here, to the effect that the maritime provinces members were called together and decided on Moncton as the terminus df this road, t This is not the case, because there are several members of the maritime provinces who never heard anything about this matter until they heard it at the Railway Committee, and therefore it was not possible for them to agree to Moncton as the terminus. Let me here say for the benefit of this committee, that there is no other possible route for this road except from Quebec via Connors and the valley of St. John river to Fredericton and thence to Chipman and St. John. I think that is the proper route, and that is the only route that can possibly be built successfully. And, so far as the harbour of St. John is concerned, it does not need any person on this committee or in this House to advocate its good qualities to those who know anything about it. It is only those who are acquainted with the harbour of St. John who will attempt to say that it is not capable of doing all the business that may be brought there.
On section 13-bond issue,

With regard to this clause, I wish to be understood as repeating the observations I made with regard to clause 4, dealing with the subject of capital stock. As I referred to this clause somewhat fully in the remarks I made, I shall not repeat here what I said, except to say that I regard the proposed capitalization of this company as altogether excessive. It seems to me that the government, in taking the responsibility of permitting the Bill to pass in this way can hardly be regarded as having given that consideration to the reasons which have been already brought to the attention of the House which I think their importance demands.
On section 15-power to make changes in steamship business,
There is a model clause for this, is there not ? Is this the usual clause ?

It is practically the same. 1 would not go so far as to say it was exactly the same. The Canadian Pacific Railway have it, the Winnipeg and Hudson's Bay have it, the Hudson's Bay and Pacific have it, and the Canada Atlantic have it.
On section 16,
The company, may purchase, lease er otherwise acquire, hold, enjoy and manage, as well in Canada as in such other places as are deemed expedient for the purposes of the company, and either in the name of the company or in the name of a trustee or trustees for the company, such lands, water lots, wharfs, docks, dock yards, slips, warehouses, elevators, offices and other buildings as it finds necessary and convenient for its purposes ; and may construct any of such works or buildings and sell or otherwise dispose thereof for the purposes of

the company ; and may carry on the business of warehousemen and wharfingers, and charge wharfage and other dues for the use of^ any such property ; and may take and hold, either in the name of the company or in the name of some person as trustee for the company, and dispose of, shares in any incorporated company having for one of its objects the exercise of any of the powers hereby conferred upon the company, and may enter into any agreements with any such company respecting the use of any of the property of such company.
2. If the company cannot agree with the owner for the purchase of any property in Canada required for wharfs, docks, dock yards, slips or elevators to he used in connection with the railway, it may cause a map or pian and book of reference to be made of such property, and all the provisions of sections 107 to 111, inclusive. of the Railway Act shall apply to the subject matter of this subsection and to the obtaining of such property and determining the compensation payable therefor.

This section seems to give very wide powers. As I understand it. it would enable this company to hold all the shares of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, or, indeed, of nil the telephone companies in the country, and all the shares of all the telegraph companies too. The words I refer to are ' and may take and hold, either in the name of the company or in the name of some person as trustee for the company, and dispose of, shares in any incorporated company having for one of its objects the exercise of any of the powers hereby conferred upon the company.'
Mr. McCarthy. The hon. member (Mr. Borden. Halifax) will see that early in the section are the words ' for the purposes of the company.' It could not be deemed expedient. for the purposes of the company, to own the whole stock of the Bell Telephone Company or of all the telegraph companies in Canada.

I do not think that quite covers what I am talking about. I will read, leaving out the unnecessary words. ' The company may purchase as well in Canada as in such other places as are deemed expedient for the purposes of the company '-the words to which the hon. gentleman refers only to places other than Canada, and the company would be ttie judge of what would he expedient. I do not at present see that the clause controls in any way, with respect to matters to which I refer.
If it is expedient.
It is only a question of place.

I think the words ' may purchase, lease or otherwise acquire, hold, enjoy and manage as well In Canada as in such other places as are deemed expedient.' are governed by the words ' for the purposes of the company' It is evidently intended to be for the pur-Mr. McCarthy. .
pose of the company. I suggest to put after the word ' manage,' ' for the purposes of the company.'

If that suggestion were carried out it would modify the meaning down to the end of the 53rd line. Then after that do you not proceed without any qualification ' and may carry on the business of warehouse men and wharfingers and charge wharfage and other dues for the use of such property'?
That is intended.

It seems to me that the words to which I call attention were not intended to give the company the absolute right to hold a majority of the shares of any telephone company. It would hardly be necessary in the interests of the promoters of the Bill to desire such wide powers as are contained in these words.

It is necessary to be careful about this, because this same form of language is creeping into a number of Bills, and no language could be broader.
Mr. McCarthy. In section 17 of the original Bill a great many larger powers were asked, and at the suggestion of the minister it was remodelled. I think that was one of the clauses that were left to be settled between the solicitor of the railway company and the minister. The clauses now in the Bill were settled. I should have thought that the objects referred to would only be the objects conferred in this section, and not the objects generally conferred iu the Bill.
Suppose we put it in that way, instead of the word ' hereby ' you say ' by this section.'
I have no objection.

What is the meaning of the words in the second line [DOT] as well in Canada as in such other places?'
Mr. McCarthy. We might need a wharf or a dock in another country besides Canada.

For what purpose ?
Mr. McCarthy. For the purpose of carrying on the business of the company.

I presume the intention is to run a steamship line to the old country.
Mr. McCarthy. Yes, or to Japan or China. Perhaps the hon. gentleman would allow this section to pass.
Let it stand and get your amendment ready.

I cannot see what advantage is to be gained by the amendment

suggested. I would rather not have the clause interfered with without consultation, if it is possible to get it through without.

My objection is this, that if you can find some company that has got a number of powers, one company in this Act, you can agree with that company as to all its powers.
And may take and hold either in the name of the company or in the name of some person as trustee for the company, and dispose of shares in any incorporate company

That is in the whole company.
-having for one of its objects the exercise of any of the powers hereby conferred upon the company.
Now, if you find a company that has got any one of the powers that this company has, you may take shares in the whole of that other company. Surely that is not intended.
This is a very usual clause. I have sent for the Joint Stock Companies Act, I think I can find it in the Joint Stock Companies Act.
Quite possibly, but I think it is very objectionable.
Still, it is to be found in all the other Bills and if it is a usual clause in the Companies Act, I do not see why we should single this out.

The position I understood the hon. member for Simcoe to take was this, that the word ' hereby ' was intended to limit the powers to the objects set forth in section 16. I said I was perfectly willing to accept that, provided it had some words that would make it perfectly plain. I was proposing to move that we strike out the word ' hereby ' and substitute the words ' by this section.'

I think there is no doubt but that they are general. If you look at subsection 2 of clause 22, they could buy up all the telegraph and telephone lines in the country if they wished to. It says :
The company may construct, maintain, control and operate telegraph and telephone lines upon and along its railway and branches ; and may establish offices for and undertake the transmission of messages for the public by any of its* lines, and collect tolls therefor ; and for any of the said purposes may enter into agreements with any other company, or may lease the company's lines or any portion thereof, and may connect its lines with the lines of any companies having authority to operate telegraph or telephone lines, and may enter into arrangements with any such companies for the exchange and transmission of messages or for the working in whole or in part of the lines of the' company.
2. The company may construct, maintain and operate any other lines of telegraph and telephone. not exceeding ojie hundred miles In length in any one case, from any point on the lines constructed or to be constructed along 164
the line of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, to connect such lines with any other lines of telegraph or telephone in Canada ; and may also construct, maintain and operate telegraph and telephone lines from its western terminus or termini to any point on Vancouver Island, and for this purpose may lay submarine lines of telegraph and telephone between such points.
That is a special power given to this company. Under that, I think there is no doubt they could buy up all the telegraph and telephone lines in the country. I remember calling attention to this clause in the committee. Although it was passed, I take the same view as the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) does that it will be general. I think it is general, and I do not see any reason why it should be required. Clause 16, is a special clause about wharfs, &c., and there is no objection about buying up steamers, and so on. I think it would be well to confine the section to the powers given in section 16. It was not intended that this company should be given the power to go and buy up telegraph and telephone lines. We have never knowingly granted in any Bills we have passed, any such power.

My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) will realize how important it is with a Bill of this character not to do anything that will have the effect of interfering with the powers that are intended to be conferred. This point was considered in the committee, and the solicitor of the company was present. This clause was a matter of special consideration, and I apprehend under the circumstances, we cannot go very far wrong by passing a clause of this description which only con-, fers powers that the general company's Act would give.
Do you find that in the General Companies Act ?
I am looking for it now.

Let the section stand and we will come back to it later on.
Section allowed to stand.
On section 17,
The company may, for the purposes of its railway and steamships and in connection with its business,-
(a.) build, purchase, lease or otherwise acquire. manage or control, at such points or places along its railway or any branch thereof, or at any ports or places of call of any of its steamships such buildings as it deems advisable for hotels and restaurants ; and may purchase, lease and hold the land necessary for such purposes ; and may carry on business in connection therewith, and afford such facilities as may tend to the comfort and convenience of the travelling public ; and may let any such building for such purposes ; and may acquire, hold and dispose of shares in any incorporated company having for one of its objects the exercise of any of the powers by this section con-



ferred upon the company, and enter into agreements with any such company respecting any of such building, lands, facilities or business ;
(b.) purchase, lease and hold lands required for, and lay out, establish and manage parks and pleasure grounds, and give a lease thereof to. or contract with, any person for the use thereof upon such terms as the company deems expedient.

I see that the phrase ' by this section conferred ' is used, while in the preceding section the word 'hereby' is used. The hon. leader of the opposition was pointing out that the words should be ' by this section.'

The language of this section is extremely comprehensive :
May acquire, hold and dispose of shares in any incorporated company having for one of Its objects the exercise of any of the powers by this section conferred upon the company.
That is quite a frequent clause.

It may be frequent, but I doubt very much the wisdom of it, because, where you have a, number of companies incorporated embracing a large number of objects, if you include in these charters language of this kind you give almost unlimited powers of amalgamation.

Section agreed to.
On section 24, subsection 2,
Is this section giving general telegraph and telephone lines usual in these railway charters ?
In connection with their business.
This does not seem to restrict it to the company's business. You give them power to collect tolls from the public, and so forth.

This matter was very carefully considered in committee. You give them the usual powers that are given to other railway companies, and then you give them power to make a line 100 miles long, but only for the purpose of connecting with other telegraph or telephone lines, and on Vancouver island the committee considered it reasonable to do that.
It is just as I said : Power to do a general telephone and telegraph business.

Within certain limits. It is quite apparent that the intention was to give them the power, in so far as their line and its branches are concerned, to have telegraph and telephone lines, and if they desire to utilize these lines for general purposes, then they have the right to do so, but governed by the General Railway Act. They get power to construct lines not exceeding 100 miles in length.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: Must they keep the poles on their own right of way ?
Yes, with the exception of the lines 100 miles in length.
What does that mean ? Does it mean that they can go up and down the streets of a municipality, provided their lines did not exeeed 100 miles in length ?
They could not without the consent of the municipality.
But they apparently can by this Bill.
But under the Railway Act, the amendment of 1899, it must be with the consent of the municipality.
But that is changed by the Bill which the solicitor of the railway has before the House.

Section agreed to.
Powers, development of lands, water power, &c. ; construction of dams and biddings for electricity ; shares in other companies ; shares in mining companies.
It seems to me these are extremely wide powers. What is the object in giving the company power, for example, to enter into mining and timber speculations ?

The hon. gentleman will find similar clauses in quite a number of charters. The idea of the committee seems to be that it has been found useful in the development of that western country to grant such powers. The Canada Eastern, The Canadian Pacific, the Toronto and Hudson Bay, the Edmonton and Slave Lake, the Port Dover, Brantford and Berlin, and the Bay of Quinte Railways have ail clauses of a similar character. So that there is ample precedent for this clause. It was very fully considered in the committee, and the form of it was somewhat changed.

I must say that I think these powers are extremely wide, whether they have been granted in other cases or not. The company is authorized to enter into the business of supplying water, and electricity for light, heat and power, provided it has a surplus of these things; and it can very easily establish a surplus if it wants to. It can also take, bold, and dispose of shares in any company incorporated for any of these purposes. It is authorized to acquire, develop, work, and dispose of mines, mining rights, timber and timber lands. It is also authorized to crush, smelt, reduce, amalgamate or otherwise treat and dispose of ores; engage in general mining and lumber operations, or in the manufacture and sale of the products thereof. It seems to me that these objects are

very foreign indeed to tlie general scope of a railway charter. However much they may have been granted to companies in the past, I 'think it is not advisable, even in the interests of the company, to confer such wide and extensive powers.
Will tlie lion, gentleman who has charge of the Bill quote a similar section to this ?

The Act to incorporate the Lake Superior and Hudson Bay Railway Company provides :
The company may, in connection with its undertaking and for the purposes of its business, erect, use. or manage, or aid and subscribe toward works, machinery and plant for the generation. transmission and distribution of electric power and energy ; acquire and utilize water powers and dispose of the same, either directly or by converting the same into electric or other power and energy.
Does that say that the company may sell its surplus power ?
No, this is much more restricted.
" This provides that the company may engage in these businesses for any other purpose than the purposes of the company.
If this company developed electricity on the line of the railway, it might be very convenient for the people in the vicinity of the railway to have an opportunity of purchasing electric light.
I think it would be very convenient, but the promoter of the Bill said that there were ample precedents for this clause. We are asking for these precedents, and we have not had them.
Does the minister think it would be advisable to authorize this company to engage in gold mining or lead mining ?

I do not think it would be very detrimental to the public interest that they should contribute to the development of mines on their line of railway, because, while they would be creating traffic for themselves, they would be contributing to works of public utility. This is not a railway through a settled part of the country, but is more in the nature of a colonization scheme.
I suppose the minister is arguing that way on the ground that this company will construct this railway with their own funds.

I like to deal with these matters as we meet them, and when we come, to the question of funds, 164}
I dare say my hon. friend will be heard from.
Sir. AIcCARTHY. In the charter of the Ottawa and Northern Railway Company it is provided :
The company may in connection with its railway and for the purposes of its undertaking,-
(a.) acquire, use, and dispose of any property, water powers and other powers, rights, easements and privileges, for the purpose of or in connection with the production, manufacture or supply of electricity for heat, light and power and for any other purpose for which the same may be used ;
(b.) produce, manufacture, use, supply and dispose of electricity for traction, light, heat and power, and for any other purpose, for which the same may be used :
(c.) locate, lease, acquire, work, and sell mines, minerals, mining rights, timber and timber landis, and develop such mines and crush, smelt, reduce, amalgamate and dispose of the ores and products of any mines, whether belonging to the company or not ; and acquire, use, and dispose of all buildings, machinery and plant requisite or necessary for carrying on or operating the said lines.

While subsection ' a ' may be restricted to some extent, it is not very much restricted at tlie end, and subsection ' b ' is not restricted at all. My bon. friend the Minister of Justice suggests that the effect of this section would be to develop the country through which the railway passes. It might have that effect, or it might have exactly the opposite effect; because a company of this kind possessing these enormous powers, in addition to having complete control over the only line of railway passing through the country, might rather tend to discourage competition. People who were disposed to enter into mining, lumbering, or smelting operations might be deterred from doing so for the very reason that an enormous corporation like this might place them rather at a disadvantage in any undertaking which they might otherwise be disposed to engage In. For example suppose you had a district in which there are coal mines. A company, which is owning practically the only railway in that section, would have an enormous advantage over any other corporation or person. It seems to me not good policy to give this company power to engage in general commercial enterprises. We might as well give it power to engage In banking or in manufacturing, which would not be much foreign to Its general undertaking with the powers conferred by this section.
The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals has always restricted such powers and I cannot see how he let this clause pass through the Railway Committee.

In the Kootenay and Arrowhead Railway Company, just the same powers were given, and that was a charter passed this session.

On section 26,
The company may construct, acquire and operate tramways or other ways for the transportation of ore and other freight.
Should not the local or municipal authorities have notice of any application under this section before the company receives power to construct such tramways.
Notice is published in the ' Gazette.'

My hon. friend knows what publication in the ' Gazette ' means. It might be published in the ' Gazette ' and none of these concerned would know anything about it.
Mr. McCarthy. The 'Gazette' is the medium by which all official notices are given. This is practically an exact copy of what was put in the Canadian Pacific Railway Bill sixty-one Victoria, chapter sixty.
This gives the copy a omnibus charter to build an electric road over the entire country.
A tramway.
A tramway may be operated by steam or by electricity.
The general Act limits it to ten miles.
Not a tramway, it limits branches to six miles, but this is not a branch but it is a regular railway.

The view of the committee was this. Tramway is a pretty well understood definition. It is something much simpler and cheaper than a railway and nobody would be foolish enough to contract it except in a new country where we would want it for temporary use before the quantity of work would justify the building of a railway. You cannot afford to build a tramway where there is any work for a railway. A tramway is not a railway. You can put a mule on it or a span of horses.
Mi\ HUGHES (Victoria). A street railway is a tramway.
No, it is a street railway, and the Electric Railway Act applies. That is the intention of putting it in at all events.
I am not so clear about that. Why would not an ordinary street railway operated by electricity be comprised within the meaning of this section ?
It is ' for the transportation of ore or other freight.'

They could not make such a road without the consent of the muni-Mr. McCarthy.
cipality. Besides, they could not carry passengers.
We should limit it to ten miles ?

This wording gives them power to construct tramways, and in some parts of Canada an ordinary street railway is called a tramway. In the maritime provinces that is quite common. In fact the electric street railway in Halifax is called a tramway, and the company that runs it is called the Halifax Electric Tramway Company. These tramways are unrestricted as to distance and may be operated by any motive power whatever. Does the hon. Minister of Justice think they are restricted V
No, I think the hon. gentleman is right.

It seems to me that it ought to be restricted in some way, as to distance at least. Otherwise the company will have a charter to build tramways all over Canada.
Mr. Hughes (Victoria). The clause read by the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. McCarthy) limited it to ten miles.

These tramways must be approved, not by Order in Council, but by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council. I think hon. gentlemen will find the same power given to the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific Railway. In a new country, very often, there is need for a cheap means of transporting freight, particularly in the mining and lumbering sections. But if you were to confine this to the carrying of ore, the company would not be free to carry back to the mines the supplies that were needed. Tram-roads are very useful, and facilities should be afforded for their consideration.

Surely, there is ample protection in the latter part of this clause. A plan must be filed with the Department of Railways and Canals and the route of the tramway must be approved by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council. It is not likely that they would allow an electric railway line entirely apart from the purposes of this road to be operated by this company. And not only that, but notice must be given by publication in the ' Canada Gazette ' and to every other company operating a railway in the locality of the intention to build one of these tramways.
Then, why not leave it to the general provisions of the Railway Act on that subject ?
That only provides for branch lines, and so there might be some question about these tram-roads.

If it is so necessary to give notice in writing to every railway company in the section, surely, if there is a municipal organization covering the railway proposed to be exploited, they should be given notice also. Why give notice to the railway company and not to the municipality ?
The provisions of the Railway Act apply.
I am asking the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. McCarthy) the question and I would like an answer from him.

Well, it is information the bon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) wants, I suppose ? He is not merely trying to trap me ? I think that the suggestion of the hon. member for South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) is right-that the Railway Act applies and that notice would have to be given. If notice were not given, and that fact were brought to the attention of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, the application would not be granted.

Surely, the hon. gentleman (Mr. McCarthy) might suggest that these words be added ' notice to be given in writing to the municipalities affected.'
Mr. McCarthy. I must say that I think there is ample protection provided in the clause.

I do not know whether there is or not, but I am bound to accept the statement of the hon. gentleman (Mr. McCarthy. But it seems to me unreasonable that the railway companies which are the creatures of this parliament are to be notified of the intention of the company to construct tramways, municipalities through which the tramways are to pass, need not be notified at all.
By the general Railway Act, they cannot commence construction without the consent of the municipalities.

While the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. McCarthy) is hunting up a clause relating to that point, I would suggest to the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick), who, I presume, is looking after the Bill in the absence of the Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair)- and I must say I think it strange that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals is not here to superintend this very important measure, but leave it to the promoter of the Bill and the Minister of Justice, neither of whom seem very familiar with the circumstances or with the clauses of the Bill- I would suggest to the Minister of Justice that a limit of length of these tramways should be introduced into this section. Ten miles, I think, was mentioned in the Bill referred to by the hon. member for Simcoe. I know that the hon. Minister of Railways
and Canals is very strong on this point. I am satisfied that this clause was not brought to his attention when it was going through the committee, or he would not have allowed the Bill to pass in the committee without fixing a limit of distance.

I think what my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) says, makes against his own argument. There must have been some cause shown why this unlimited power should be given. It was allowed to go through the committee without change, and, I do not know of any argument having been advanced for changing it.
Will the hon. Minister of Justice say that the rights of municipalities will be protected under the clause without amendment ?

I was going to say that it very frequently happens that municipalities are interested in application made before the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, and as a member of that committee I see that municipalities are invariably represented. I was just looking through the Railway Act to see under what section they are notified, but I do not see anything making it necessary to notify the municipality, except as the public are notified through the ' Canada Gazette.'

I would ask the hon. minister if he does not think it passing strange, to say the least of it. that the railway companies must be specially notified, while the municipalities, which certainly are as much interested in the construction of these trams, are not to be notified ? Aim, is there anything unreasonable in suggesting that, in those places where the company proposes to extend its line, the municipalities, if there are any, should be notified. I think the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. McCarthy) is looking over the existing Act to see whether the interested municipalities in this respect are protected or not. But may I ask the Minister of Justice if the Railway Committee of the Privy Council will not be superseded by the Bill that is now passing through the House under the direction of the Minister of Railways and Canals ?
Yes, it will.

There are provisions in that Bill which give extraordinary power. And when -(if I may be permitted to refer to the matter now)-when some of its clauses were being considered, we were told that the way to protect the rights of municipalities was by provisions in the special Acts that are passed in this House from time to time. I am sure the hon. Minister of Justice will bear testimony to that. If it is not a hardship that the railway companies who may be interested are to be notified, surely, it cannot be a hardship to make

It necessary that the municipalities through which these trams are to be constructed, shall be notified, and, if they have objections to offer, that they may be heard. I would like also to ask what is the meaning of the words ' other ways ' in the first line of this section, which reads, 'the company may construct, acquire and operate tramways or other ways ? '

The obvious intention of this section is simply to enable them to carry freight and supplies to and from the camp, or from any mining properties. The question raised by the hon. gentleman would never come up. .Wherever there is a municipality organized there are always other methods provided for carrying freight.
There are municipalities in the older sections of Ontario, densely populated, that have no tramways at all.

I say where there is a municipality there are other means of transporting supplies in and out, such as by ordinary cartage. In a locality where lumbering operations are carried on, the simplest plan is to put in a tramway. That is all that is contemplated here.

I am satisfied that the words ' or other ways ' would allow the construction of a railway.
Mr. McCarthy. Then the General Railway Act comes in.
You can build a railway six miles long without the authority of the Railway Act, and this will give the company permission to build a line 100 miles long, if they wish.
If it was a railway it would come under the operation of the Railway Act.

Any railway company can build a branch six miles long without having the word ' branch ' mentioned in its charter. But when you want to build a branch line from any point to any other point, they are always put in the Bill. Now, not only do we limit the number of miles these branches should be constructed, but the minister is particular to have the places mentioned from which they start and to which they go. That is not done in this Bill at all.
Does the Minister of Justice say that under this clause the rights of municipalities are fully protected ?

I think that under this clause, with the General Railway Act, the municipalities would be protected. I would not consider it possible for a moment that the Railway Committee would consider a question in which the interest of a municipality was concerned without notice having been given to the municipality.
Should there not be some restriction as to the length of these tramways ? Is it desirable to give an unlimited right as to distance ?

I apprehend, speaking somewhat without knowledge, that the intention of the company was to have tramways constructed for the purpose of enabling them to communicate with the mines and other works of that description, and that they wanted to erect cheap means of conveyance to get to them. I apprehend that is what they have in view. It was never intended to give to the company the right to do anything except to operate such lines or ways of communication.

If this road was running through the British Columbia mountains and there was a mine fifteen or twenty miles away, under this Bill they need not come here for any authority, for this would give them power to build a track.

They could not go one inch beyond the line of their railway without having some autlior-tiy from this parliament to do so. I am willing to defer absolutely to the opinion of the leader of the opposition on that point.
Supposing there is a mining company in one of these valleys, and in order to get that ore out it is necessary to build a wooden tramway. Is it necessary to come to this House to get a charter ?
The mining company might do that if they choose, but the railway company could not do it.
Could 'not they go twenty miles on their own land ?	[DOT]
Of course they could on their own land, but I say they could not go beyond their own right of way. But I do not anticipate they would own twenty miles on each side of the road.
They have power to buy for the purposes of the company.
On their own land they can do it. They might buy all the land in the neighbourhood for the purpose of reaching this mine.
Hon. gentlemen see that it only applies to ore or freight. It cannot be considered, therefore, to be a railway.
In the Canadian Pacific Railway Bill they are limited to ten miles.

In British Columbia
we would be very glad if the company could
extend its line twenty miles beyond the

main line in order to reach a mine. We won't kick in British Columbia.
Make it fifty miles if necessary, but let us have some restriction.

I suppose the object is to get freight. If it is fifty miles by tramway what is the difference, so long as they are opening up the country, and getting freight? Tt helps every body, no body is going to be injured. It is in the interest of the railway, in the interest of the company and in the interest of the mining.
What is the meaning of the words ' for the transportation of ore and other freight ' ? Would not that give them the right to construct the tramway for the purpose of bringing other freight ?
It would permit them to build a tramway or any other way on which to carry ore, or freight of any kind, such as lumber.
Will the hon. gentleman say as a legal gentleman that this section would confine the construction of these tramways to the mountainous country, or a country where mining was going on ?
I should think so.
What about hauling grain on tramways in the prairie section, hauling any agricultural produce ?
There might be such a case. But if it was nothing but a tramway, what is the difference, even if you carry grain of any kind, provided you help the people in that district ?
Then the idea is that this is not to be confined to mining countries, and that a tram can be built on any part of this line to an unlimited length.
To carry ores and freight, any supplies to the mines or out of them.

The member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser)) is very plausible. He may take the same stand here to-night as in every Bill that has been before this House for years. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals has been very particular to limit this to certain distances.
That is the railway.

No, not the
railway. The railway could only go six miles without special permission. We are giving them power to build a tramway.
No.

We are certainly giving them power to build a trainwav. The words ' other way ' will include a railway.
Mr. FRASER, No.
A railway is another way.
No, no.
What is it then?
It is a lesser way than a tramway.
No, I understand the meaning of the English language as well as the hon. member for Guysborough does.
But not the Gaelic.
I do not know about the Gaelic-perhaps the Gaelic, too.
That would be putting the greater before the less.

We have clauses drawn by lawyers with the idea of obtaining certain powers without having to come back here for them. I maintain that every solitary station along the main line and branches of that road could have its tramway or electric road.
Mr. McCarthy. Subject to the approval of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council.

Everything is subject to the Railway Committee of the Privy Council. They have to file their plans before they can build a branch of any kind. They can build an electric road from every station along the line.

Is it reasonable to make a statement of that kind ? When they come before the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, is it reasonable to suppose that such a state of affairs would exist ? It cannot possibly exist. You have to keep in mind what is intended by the clause. It specifically says for the purpose of getting out ore or other freight.
Or other freight, which means everything.
Jurisdiction is given to the Railway Committee of the Privy Council to sanction this power.

Is it intended that the jurisdiction of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council shall be perpetuated after the railway commission is appointed ? I do not know whether the railway committee is to be abolished or not.
As I understand it, this railway commission will have jurisdiction, and the matter will then be in the hands of independent persons.

Lawyers for these railway companies-I care not whether it is the Grand Trunk Pacific, or the Canadian Pacific Railway, or the Canadian Northern-draft these Bills in such a way that

they get all the powers it is possible for them to get. They are a perfect nuisance at the Railway Committee, as every one knows.
Do not be offensive.
Every one knows it.
No, no.

I know it is hard on the lawyers, but it is the only chance we have of getting even with them. I think this clause should be held over until we get the opinion of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, who does know something about railway legislation.

I would be content with the opinion of the hon. Minister of Justice. I want to be clear myself, personally, as to the meaning of this word ' tramway,' how far it extends, and what powers are given to the company to construct tramways. I am prepared to take an expression of opinion from the hon. Minister of Justice in respect to the matter.

I understand it to mean purely and simply that wheii you give to this railway company these facilities for collecting freight, in my judgment, you substitute this for the ordinary method of collecting freight by means of vehicles and horses.
