Under this clause would this railway company have authority to construct a tramway or other way from any of its stations to run 30, 40 or 50 miles across the prairies or up the mountain valleys for the collection of freight ?
I cannot see that there is any limit put upon their right here.
This road, I understand, will run into the ancient city of Quebec, of which the hon. Minister of Justice is the representative.
I hope it will.
I understand it is going down there. I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Justice if this company will have the right to construct tramways in Quebec city ?
No.
Or in any other city ?
No.
Why not ?

I consider that the municipality would have sufficient control to prevent that being done without the consent of the municipality having first been obtained. That is a power that would Mr. HUGHES (Victoria).
have to be exercised subject to the decision of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council.

I hope the hon. Minister of Justice will assist us when the general Railway Bill is being considered in insisting that the board of railway commissioners to be appointed shall not have power to override the rights of municipalities in this matter.

In all fairness, the matter should be considered, and the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals should be consulted in connection with this question. I know he objects to this provision. In this Bill there is a clause limiting the company in the location of its main line to a line 30 miles away from another main line. Under this section that 30 miles is wiped out entirely. The company may construct tramways from every station along the line as far as they choose to go. These tramways would constitute a railway, in which event they would come under the general Railway Act.

I would like, with the permission of the committee, to call the attention of the hon. Minister of Justice to a section that will probably be embodied in the General Railway Act, which makes provision that a railway may be carried along or across any existing highway, leave having first been obtained from the board as hereinafter provided. The Railway Committee of the Privy Council have now the power to give all of these rights which are being asked for in this clause ; and the Board of Railway Commissioners, under the new Railway Act, can give the right to this company to construct a tramway upon, over, or across any highway, the only condition being that they shall not obstruct the passage of vehicles or close up the entrance to a man's house. I would like to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Justice to this clause, in view of the proposed clause that is going into the Railway Act. We are trying to prepare an amendment to section 184, of the Railway Bill to meet the views of those who believe that the rights of municipalities should not be taken away from them.
It has been suggested that the word ' ways ' might mean rope walks.
Would it not mean waterways ?	[DOT]
Or any other kind of way.
Would it not mean a waterway ?	[DOT]
It could not mean a waterway, seriously.
Why not ?

It is not
limited in its construction.
Mr. HUGHES {Victoria). This clause should be allowed to stand.

In view of the extraordinary privileges we are giving the company, it is "not unreasonable that we should be able to understand exactly what rights are to be reserved to this railway commission and whether the municipalities are going to be protected. Unless I have the opinion of the Minister of Justice to the contrary, I shall rest firmly under the opinion that this clause practically filches from every municipality in the country the light to protest against any tramway coming in, along or upon its highway, without its consent.
I do not like to commit myself to a legal opinion without considering it, and giving an opinion which I think would be of some value.
It is because we place so much reliance in the opinion of the Minister of Justice that we wish to proceed slowly and let this clause stand.

I am not in charge of .the Bill.
Mr. McCarthy. Let it stand.
Section allowed to stand.
On section 27,
May I ask what is the idea of including the word ' mills ' in this section ?
The precedent for this is to be found in 2 Edward VII, chapter 15, an Act relating to the Canadian Northern Railway Company.
That does not give the company power to operate mills.
When I said a moment ago that this company might be allowed to engage in banking business, I did not know there was something approaching it. I see they are allowed to make advances to settlers.
That is a loan company.
Yes. What is the meaning of having the word ' mills ' here.
I think I would drop the word ' mills ' myself.
I would be inclined to drop it also.

It has been found very desirable that railway companies should have that power. For instance, it would be in the interest of the company and in the interest of the settlers to have a saw mill. Some railway companies have come back for amendments to
include this power, and this is confined for the purposes of the company.
There is nothing in this clause about the purposes of the company.
I think this section applies only to the purpose of the company. I think the Canadian Pacific came back to get legislation to enable it to encourage mining by going into smelting.
All the clauses the hon. gentleman lias referred to in other charters have been for the purposes of the company.
This clause would be a distinct advantage to the country in promoting settlement; but perhaps mills might be cut off.
Mills are very necessary.

The other clause was not changed, but this clause was discussed at length in the Railway Committee, and we amended it subject to the approval of the Minister of Railways; and in view of the precedents which I have referred to, I think I am not unreasonable in asking that it should be allowed to pass in the form in which it now is.
Have the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian Northern power to construct mills ?
They have power to construct mills, and as a matter of fact they are operating lumber mills.

The word is not restricted in any way in this clause, so that the company might operate woollen mills or cotton mills. The hon. gentleman had better accept the suggestion of the Minister of Justice, and strike that word out.
Mr. McCarthy. I do not think the hon. gentleman should ask me to do that. If we were a thousand miles from nowhere, the company would have to get timber to construct bridges, and it is only fair that it should have power to operate mills.

Under that clause it might have all the mills in creation-saw mills, woollen mills, cotton mills, gin mills, and every other kind of mills. I think the hon. gentleman should take the suggestion of the Minister of Justice and drop the word ' mills.'
Any railway company can put up a mill for its own purposes. We do not want; provision for that in the statute.	*	"
If we were four or five hundred miles away in the country, and our own mill was constructed, the hon. gentleman would not say that we could not give settlers the advantage of it.

But this section apparently would authorize the operation of a woollen mill or a cotton mill in the city of Quebec. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice might find some difficulty in his own constituency when some of his own supporters were met with the competition of this company by the erection of some of its mills there.

I think the development of the west owes a great deal to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company for erecting saw mills and for building smelters to' encourage the mining industry, when private capital would not do it. I think no possible harm could result, but it would be greatly to the interest of the country, if this power were given to this company. There is no iuteution, of course, to start woollen mills or cotton mills, but for these two particular purposes which I have mentioned, I think it is necessary that it should have that power.
If you would confine the meaning of the clause to saw mills, there would be no objection.

The first words in the section control its meaning .	' The company
may, for the purpose of promoting the settlement and cultivation of any lands served by its railway or branch lines.' Everything is subject to promoting settlement and cultivating land.

If the hon. gentleman will read the whole clause, he will see that it does not bear that interpretation. If this is to be a railway company, it should not go into milling and manufactures of all kinds. There ought to be some limit.
I think that this clause ought to stand. It also authorizes the railway to be a trust and loan company.

We will limit the clause to saw mills and grist mills and other similar works.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 35-Power to acquire stock in other companies.

This is a very extraordinary power, is it not ? I would ask the Minister of Justice what he thinks about it. Does it not confer unusually wide power, and is it not in direct contravention of a clause of the Railway Act ?

Under 2 Edward vii, chapter 46, section 15, it is provided ;-
The company may acquire, hold and dispose of stock and"'bonds in any other company, provided that such powers shall not be exercised unless and until the directors have been expressly authorized by a by-law passed by them for the purpose and sanctioned by a vote of not less than two-thirds in value of the shareholders present or represented by proxy at a special or general meeting of the company duly Mr. McCarthy.
called for the purpose of considering the subject of such by-law, and such by-law shall be subject to the approval of the Governor in Council.
What company received these powers ?
The Canada Eastern.

But the hon. gentleman (Mr. McCarthy) knows that there is a clause in the General Railway Act prohibiting a railway company from acquiring stock of another railway company under a penalty of $1,000 against any director who takes part in such a transaction. A provision such as the hon. gentleman has read, may have crept into one special Act, but this general clause is to prevent the very thing .so permitted. The object is to prevent railway companies from buying up the stock of other companies appointing friendly boards and so doing away with competition. This was discussed on Friday last, and I think the Minister of Railways and Canals approved of that provision in the General Railway Act. The provision inserted in this Bill would enable this company to buy up all the small lines on its route, even provinical railways, and do away with all competition.
This penalty is against a director, if he makes this purchase with the funds of the company.
As a director, it could only be with the funds of the company.
But one director could not bind another.
But this enables a company to buy with its own funds stock in other railway companies to an unlimited extent.

I fancy the clause referred to in the General Railway Act is clause 276, which provides :-
No company shall, either directly or indirectly, employ any of its funds in the purchase of its own stock, or in the acquisition of any shares, lands or other securities issued by any other railway company in Canada.
And the clause following, No. 277, provides for the penalty.

The reason certain companies were allowed to acquire stock in other companies was because they had obtained long, almost perpetual leases and afterwards were allowed to acquire the stocks. But the object of the general provision is manifestly to prevent one company buying up another and so doing away with competition.
In view of this general provision can this section be read as applying to any railway company ?

Why not
make it clear by saying 'any company not
being a railway company ' ?
The general section provides that this shall not be done, but only excludes companies which have the power. It does not cover companies which may hereafter acquire power.

I am afraid that would hardly do. It says :
But this shall not affect the powers or rights which any company in Canada now has or possesses by virtue of any special Act

And so on, that Act must be read in the present, and would be considered applicable to companies that got special Acts of parliament, I think. It would be better to adopt the suggestion of the Minister of Finance and insert words excluding railway companies.
Why not leave it over and look into the matter ? But even then they could buy up a bank or any other company.
I was just going to suggest that.
I was going to ask my hon. friend who runs the financial end of the government whether they could do that in the case of a bank.
They could buy up the stock.

Shall the section read :-
The company may acquire, hold, guarantee, pledge and dispose of stocks and bonds or other securities of any company other than a railway company, upon such terms

And so on ? Carried.

I want this carried on a division, for I object to the principle of any company being allowed to buy stock in another company. I dq not wish to obstruct the objects of this company, but I do not see why it is necessary to grant such a power, and I object to the principle of any railway company or any other company being granted such extensive powers as these.

Section agreed to, on division.
On section 31, subsection 3,
The company may unite with, or enter into any agreement with any other company, corporation or person for the construction or maintenance of any such bridge and the approaches thereto, as a joint work, or for the joint working, control, management and use thereof.

In regard to this section, I beg to suggest to the government, not to the promoter of the Bill, that in the construction of any bridge across any large streams in the North-west, or any part of the country where the railway company gets a subsidy, the government should see to it that the bridge is constructed so that it may be a passenger bridge as well as a
railway bridge, and that the bridge should either be free or the tolls should be fixed low.
On section 32,

We have in the past added to a number of Bills some provision respecting passes through the mountains, that where there is only room for one road the other companies should have the right to use the tracks of the pioneer company. We have done that year after year in all roads going through mountain passes.
